extraction.body: Apple today announced HomeView, a $299 smart home display with a 7-inch screen that lets users control connected accessories, make FaceTime calls, and enjoy music and video content. But what about third-party apps? Here’s what Apple says. Apple says the new HomeView smart home display is “designed for life at home,” with a wide range of features for managing connected accessories, staying organized, and enjoying entertainment. That includes everything from controlling smart home devices and checking calendars to watching videos, listening to music, and making FaceTime calls. However, one question Apple’s announcement didn’t fully answer is the extent to which HomeView will support third-party apps. According to Apple, in addition to a selection of Apple apps, including Music, Podcasts, and Safari, HomeView will also support “compatible third-party audio and video apps from your iPhone for a familiar experience across devices.” Interestingly, the fine print for this feature differs between Apple’s HomeView marketing page and the product’s press release. The press release , however, includes an additional detail (emphasis ours): Subscription may be required to access some content and services. Some applications are not available in all areas. Select apps require a paired and compatible iPhone nearby. Some of Apple’s own first-party apps will also be available from the iPhone, the company notes. That includes Audiobooks, Apple Music Classical, News, and TV. Apple has yet to detail how the iPhone proximity requirement will work, and whether developers of apps in supported categories will need to take any additional steps to support HomeView. Not trying to be the negative Nancy here but does this actually look like a useful product that will sell much outside of the apple customer that needs to get anything they put out? I know some have talked in the past about wanting something in the kitchen but what does this do that an iPad can't do for those needs? If this came out 15+ years ago, I could see it catching on for awhile before people realized they could get other devices to do what it does better. Apple is usually good with knowing their markets so I guess we'll see. This just feels like it's going against the direction of everything else. Most desktop computer users went to laptops, tablets, and phones already meaning having a static device and going mobile...or so I thought. According ot Wired , “a handful of third-party media apps like Spotify are available, and developers can bring over existing CarPlay apps.” Wired adds that “if your iPhone already has one of these CarPlay apps installed, it can automatically appear on the HomeView after setup.” So it looks like HomeView’s third-party app support will rely on the existing CarPlay framework, rather than requiring developers to build apps specifically for the device. It remains unclear, though, whether this will extend to other CarPlay app categories, such as communication and AI assistants, or also be limited to media apps. We have reached out to Apple for clarification on how third-party app support will work, and will update this post if we hear back. Are you getting an Apple HomeView? Let us know in the comments. extraction.body: I never thought Apple would launch a smart display . Apple has been historically late to the game in the smart-home world, if it bothers showing up at all. It’s had the most minimal smart speaker (and general smart home) offerings of any of the major brands, with just the HomePod and HomePod mini compared with the variety of speakers and smart home products Amazon and Google have launched in the past decade. A limited selection isn't necessarily a bad thing, but the Apple HomePods have also never excelled in our testing, either, and Apple's overall ecosystem has had the most limited compatibility compared with other devices (though Matter is helping expand that). With the HomeView's arrival, Apple is making its first foray into the smart display category, nearly 10 years after Amazon’s first Echo Show model. While the HomeView manages to do some things well, it's once again a product made for only the biggest of Apple enthusiasts, and will shine best for users who have an iCloud subscription, love Apple Music, and will invest in Apple’s new, larger smart-home ecosystem , which has been designed in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric. The HomeView does feel handy to use for making calls and sending texts—more so than any Amazon Echo Show ever was—and I love that I can use it to find my iPhone when I lose it around the house. Still, I'd love to have been more impressed at this price point. After nearly two weeks of using the HomeView in my house, I find I use it most as a smart-home controller and to answer quick questions, and occasionally to FaceTime someone. Siri struggled to complete some of my music requests and took a long time to think about simple questions. Plus, some features on the device overall were roadblocked by my not having a full commitment to iCloud and Apple Photos. It's a device primarily for Apple devotees—especially the ones who will buy all of Apple's new smart-home products. The most surprising thing to me is how small this device is. Maybe I've been overly influenced by the announcement of Amazon’s Echo Show 16 , which has a generous 16-inch display (hence the name), but the HomeView screen is just 7 inches and square, giving it a different look from most other smart displays, which go for a rectangular design. My colleague Julian Chokkattu described it as a “giant Apple Watch,” and I agree. The swiping side to side to switch between 10 different preloaded faces and the menu bar also feel incredibly similar to the Apple Watch. Pressing and holding on the face of the HomeView allows you to customize your various “faces” (or remove them—it's a lot of options to have preloaded, in my opinion, and I found myself swiping through too frequently to find the smart home page). You can also click on the plus button to add other faces or informational pages like weather and views of your home cameras. But that's all you can add, at least for now. There's no app store, but the device can reflect certain apps from your phone, along with general apps you'd find on an Apple device like Safari, FaceTime, Messages, Find My, Alarms, and more. I was surprised to see Spotify, Libby, and Yoto specifically ported over from my phone, but no other non-Apple apps have made it over so far, at least from my own collection of downloaded apps. There isn't a Siri AI app on the HomeView like on my iPhone, but the HomeView does use Siri AI to power its intelligence and answer your questions. You'll get a more conversational response than regular Siri, but I didn't find its answers to be that much more impressive. Siri ran into issues playing my music—it asks me whether the music should come from Books, TikTok, or Spotify if I don't specify, and then most of the time it still can't play the song on Spotify, even with my account set up. It also couldn't use Find My to find my iPhone when I asked. Both of these applications worked perfectly fine on the HomeView screen itself, but the on-device Siri isn't blowing me away thus far. In fact, most things worked better by touch than voice. Spotify voice requests didn't seem to work, but the Spotify app on the device worked fine, as did using the handoff feature to send Spotify music from my phone to the HomeView. The Find My feature also didn't work over voice command—when I called my phone the same name I had seen it referred to on the HomeView while playing music, it claimed I had no device under that name. However, tapping the Find My app on the HomeView let me find my phone in a list of devices and tap it to make it start going off. While I'm bummed Siri won't let me just voice-request it, I am thrilled to have a faster way to find my iPhone lost in my house than pulling up iCloud.com. I tested the HomeView with both an iPhone Air and an older iPhone 16 Pro , but you'll want a newer phone like the Air (or 17 Pro , 18 Pro , or iPhone Duo ) to get the most out of HomeView and Siri, since that's what gives you access to the expressive, customizable Siri voices. Switching to my original phone left me stuck with a boring Siri voice that I can't customize like I could when using the iPhone Air. No matter which phone you use, you'll also need to update your phone's operating system to OS 27.2.1 in order to set up and connect to the HomeView (which also brings Siri AI onto your phone, much to my husband's chagrin). The main appeal of the HomeView, at least in my opinion, is the fact that it can control your smart-home devices with touch or voice. This is especially relevant since Apple is r olling out a larger smart-home ecosystem , with several devices coming later this year as part of its Apple Home Collection, including indoor and outdoor cameras, a smart thermostat, a video doorbell, a smart lock, and a couple of sensors. You can already control any Apple Home–compatible device on the HomeView, though, without needing Apple's lineup to release. The HomeView provides a similar experience to other smart displays , with a page you can swipe to for accessing all of the devices set up through your Apple Home app. It's easy to see the devices and quickly control them. Apple Home's biggest issue, though, continues to be compatibility. Many smart devices are only Amazon- and Google-compatible, though Matter is fixing some of that issue; I was able to connect the Ikea Varmblixt ($100) smart lamp to my Apple Home app thanks to the Matter compatibility. It was fast and seamless to control once set up, both over voice and touch. You can also touch to access your texts and FaceTime your contacts with the HomeView, which has been a pretty smooth experience for me. What's most interesting, though, is how the HomeView will verify that it's only you looking at your text messages. If it sees that someone else in your family is trying to look at or access your texts, it'll prompt that family member to switch over to their own account. It only works if they're alone in range of the device's camera, though; if they're peeking over your shoulder, access won't be denied. Apple isn't using FaceID for this, surprisingly enough. It uses biometric data to figure out who's asking via a protected part of the processor Apple calls the Secure Exclave . It's a new technology that's also on the Apple Watch ; we'll have to see how it pans out in real time. Of course, we can't talk about a smart display and speaker without talking about one of the key features: the speaker. Sound is a big part of the enjoyment from this device, and while I enjoyed the audio quality, I found it frustrating to voice-request a song. When I asked for music without prompting which app it should come from, Siri asked me if I'd like it to come from Books, TikTok, or Spotify. And when I would request a song on Spotify, Siri would say I needed to “unlock my device,” but didn't specify if that needed to happen on my iPhone or my HomeView. Or it would simply tell me there was a problem and tell me to try again. This is a huge bummer for my day-to-day use: I have a 4-year-old who loves making his own music requests and has gotten excellent at asking Google to play his latest favorite song (we're finally coming off of him requesting “Ghostbusters” and "This Is Halloween" on a daily basis). Ultimately, the easiest way to play music as a Spotify user was using the handoff feature. The HomeView has a proximity-sharing feature similar to when you tap two iPhones to AirDrop a photo or other information, and it was much, much easier to pull up a song on my iPhone and simply place it near the HomeView to send what I was listening to to the speaker. I did really like that experience, but I think Spotify users will prefer other smart speakers if music playback is a primary feature they’re looking for. The sound itself was pretty good; I was happy jamming from a range of music, whether an autumn lo-fi mix or “The Call of the Mountains,” by Eluveitie. My long-time favorite song, “Dark Blue,” by Jack's Mannequin, sounded as clear with its piano keys and background drums as it did back in 2007 when I first started listening to it. The HomeView’s audio comes from the cylinder-like base that's only about 3 inches wide, giving it a slimmer profile than most smart display bases and even just stand-alone small smart speakers (the Google Home Speaker is about 5 inches at its widest point, for comparison). Inside that base sit two full-range drivers, a down-firing woofer that promises Spatial Audio, and two force-canceling passive radiators to build out the sound. So, would I tell you to buy this? Only if you're a total Apple devotee who would use all of your preferred, Apple-run apps in tandem with the Apple HomeView. But it's really best if you're looking to invest in an Apple-run smart home (or already have one) and want a touchscreen to control it with. Or love FaceTiming so much you want an extra device for it. Otherwise, you'd be just as happy with cheaper smart displays or a simple smart speaker. Power up with unlimited access to WIRED . So, would I tell you to buy this? Only if you're a total Apple devotee who would use all of your preferred, Apple-run apps in tandem with the Apple HomeView. But it's really best if you're looking to invest in an Apple-run smart home (or already have one) and want a touchscreen to control it with. Or love FaceTiming so much you want an extra device for it. Otherwise, you'd be just as happy with cheaper smart displays or a simple smart speaker.

extraction.body: After I published my review of the HomeView, Apple’s first smart display, y’all still had a ton of questions about how it works as a smart speaker. So, I spent a bunch more time testing its audio capabilities and support for third-party music apps — and found a few more frustrations along the way. Here are the answers to all your burning questions. The HomeView isn’t a replacement for a Sonos One, a full-size HomePod, or a similar-size speaker. In size and sound, the HomeView is closer to the HomePod Mini. I tested it alongside the Mini 2 (which sounds marginally better than the first-gen Mini) and found the tabletop HomeView mostly comparable, with these caveats: The HomeView has better bass and is slightly louder, but it’s not as clear and is less room-filling. You can hear them both in action in this video, alongside the full-size HomePod, the Sonos One, and the wall-mounted HomeView: [Video: Apple HomeView Smart Speaker Audio Testing] The difference comes down to the hardware. The Mini 2 has a single full-range driver and two passive radiators, whereas the tabletop HomeView has two drivers in the display, plus a woofer and two passive radiators in its base. While the woofer adds some oomph, the HomeView’s display, which sits over the speaker base, partly covers it, affecting the sound compared to the Mini. Apple added an accelerometer to the display because tilting it changes the sound, so HomeView adjusts its EQ in real time based on the angle. Still, the Mini, while not as loud, fills a room better, thanks partly to its 360-degree sound. (The HomeView supports Spatial Audio with Dolby Atmos, which the Mini 2 doesn’t.) The wall-mounted HomeView has only two drivers, with computational audio Apple says is “tuned specifically for on-wall placement.” It sounds fine but is noticeably thinner than the tabletop version, and bass is basically non-existent. I wouldn’t recommend it for its sound quality, but it’s great for talking to a visitor through your video doorbell. Can you pair two HomeViews for stereo sound? [Image: Two HomeViews can’t be paired for stereo sound, as the HomePod Minis can. While you can group HomeViews with any other AirPlay speakers to play music out of them all at once, you can’t pair two for a stereo setup or pair a HomeView with a HomePod or Mini. I like the sound of two Minis paired in stereo and use this setup in my office and my bedroom. They also work as speakers for my Apple TVs in those rooms. If you have $300 to spend on a good-sounding smart speaker setup, go with two Minis over a HomeView. I cover its uses extensively in my full review, but for audio in particular, I like that the screen acts like a jukebox, making it easy to change songs, select new music, and scroll through your podcasts or audiobooks — without needing to find a quarter! You can AirPlay to the HomeView as with any other AirPlay speaker, and audio handoff works the same as it does on HomePods. Tap your phone to the HomeView, and whatever is playing transfers to the speakers and the screen. Handoff also works in reverse, letting you send any content back to your phone. YouTube and YouTube TV videos also handed off, even though they don’t have an app on the HomeView. But Netflix and Amazon Prime Video only played audio, though both played video in the Safari browser. As with HomePods, if you’re holding your phone within a few inches, the HomeView will try to hand off content. However, you can play audio to any AirPlay speaker or group of speakers. I tested this on HomePods, Sonos speakers, and a Samsung TV, and it worked smoothly. For native apps (Apple Music, Podcasts, and Safari), the HomeView remembers the last speaker or speaker pair you used and automatically plays content through those when you return. Things get messier with third-party audio apps such as Spotify and Audible, and with Apple apps that use the CarPlay interface, such as Apple News and Apple TV. The HomeView only automatically uses the last speakers if you choose content from the HomeView screen. If you use Siri voice control, it defaults to the HomeView speaker. So, “Hey Siri, play ‘Femininomenon’ by Chappell Roan from Spotify” played music from HomeView’s speaker and not the stereo pair of Minis in my office, where I’d last been listening to Spotify. I could direct it to play music there by adding “on Office,” but that’s more of a mouthful than just “Hey Siri, play ‘Femininomenon’ by Chappell Roan,” which is all you need to say if you use Apple Music. Which brings me to another one of your most-asked questions — and my biggest complaint about this device as a smart speaker: How does it support third-party audio apps? Apple has taken a shortcut here: Rather than building a dedicated HomeView experience for app developers, the HomeView uses Apple’s existing CarPlay platform. This makes it easier for developers to put their apps on the HomeView — if an audio or video app supports CarPlay, it already works on the HomeView (there’s no support for other types of CarPlay apps). In practice, this creates frustrating limitations, including no search function and the need for a user profile on the HomeView and your phone on the same Wi-Fi.

extraction.body: I never thought Apple would launch a smart display . Apple has been historically late to the game in the smart-home world, if it bothers showing up at all. It’s had the most minimal smart speaker (and general smart home) offerings of any of the major brands, with just the HomePod and HomePod mini compared with the variety of speakers and smart home products Amazon and Google have launched in the past decade. A limited selection isn't necessarily a bad thing, but the Apple HomePods have also never excelled in our testing, either, and Apple's overall ecosystem has had the most limited compatibility compared with other devices (though Matter is helping expand that). With the HomeView's arrival, Apple is making its first foray into the smart display category, nearly 10 years after Amazon’s first Echo Show model. While the HomeView manages to do some things well, it's once again a product made for only the biggest of Apple enthusiasts, and will shine best for users who have an iCloud subscription, love Apple Music, and will invest in Apple’s new, larger smart-home ecosystem , which has been designed in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric. The HomeView does feel handy to use for making calls and sending texts—more so than any Amazon Echo Show ever was—and I love that I can use it to find my iPhone when I lose it around the house. Still, I'd love to have been more impressed at this price point. After nearly two weeks of using the HomeView in my house, I find I use it most as a smart-home controller and to answer quick questions, and occasionally to FaceTime someone. Siri struggled to complete some of my music requests and took a long time to think about simple questions. Plus, some features on the device overall were roadblocked by my not having a full commitment to iCloud and Apple Photos. It's a device primarily for Apple devotees—especially the ones who will buy all of Apple's new smart-home products. The most surprising thing to me is how small this device is. Maybe I've been overly influenced by the announcement of Amazon’s Echo Show 16 , which has a generous 16-inch display (hence the name), but the HomeView screen is just 7 inches and square, giving it a different look from most other smart displays, which go for a rectangular design. My colleague Julian Chokkattu described it as a “giant Apple Watch,” and I agree. The swiping side to side to switch between 10 different preloaded faces and the menu bar also feel incredibly similar to the Apple Watch. Pressing and holding on the face of the HomeView allows you to customize your various “faces” (or remove them—it's a lot of options to have preloaded, in my opinion, and I found myself swiping through too frequently to find the smart home page). You can also click on the plus button to add other faces or informational pages like weather and views of your home cameras. But that's all you can add, at least for now. There's no app store, but the device can reflect certain apps from your phone, along with general apps you'd find on an Apple device like Safari, FaceTime, Messages, Find My, Alarms, and more. I was surprised to see Spotify, Libby, and Yoto specifically ported over from my phone, but no other non-Apple apps have made it over so far, at least from my own collection of downloaded apps. There isn't a Siri AI app on the HomeView like on my iPhone, but the HomeView does use Siri AI to power its intelligence and answer your questions. You'll get a more conversational response than regular Siri, but I didn't find its answers to be that much more impressive. Siri ran into issues playing my music—it asks me whether the music should come from Books, TikTok, or Spotify if I don't specify, and then most of the time it still can't play the song on Spotify, even with my account set up. It also couldn't use Find My to find my iPhone when I asked. Both of these applications worked perfectly fine on the HomeView screen itself, but the on-device Siri isn't blowing me away thus far. In fact, most things worked better by touch than voice. Spotify voice requests didn't seem to work, but the Spotify app on the device worked fine, as did using the handoff feature to send Spotify music from my phone to the HomeView. The Find My feature also didn't work over voice command—when I called my phone the same name I had seen it referred to on the HomeView while playing music, it claimed I had no device under that name. However, tapping the Find My app on the HomeView let me find my phone in a list of devices and tap it to make it start going off. While I'm bummed Siri won't let me just voice-request it, I am thrilled to have a faster way to find my iPhone lost in my house than pulling up iCloud.com. I tested the HomeView with both an iPhone Air and an older iPhone 16 Pro , but you'll want a newer phone like the Air (or 17 Pro , 18 Pro , or iPhone Duo ) to get the most out of HomeView and Siri, since that's what gives you access to the expressive, customizable Siri voices. Switching to my original phone left me stuck with a boring Siri voice that I can't customize like I could when using the iPhone Air. No matter which phone you use, you'll also need to update your phone's operating system to OS 27.2.1 in order to set up and connect to the HomeView (which also brings Siri AI onto your phone, much to my husband's chagrin). The main appeal of the HomeView, at least in my opinion, is the fact that it can control your smart-home devices with touch or voice. This is especially relevant since Apple is r olling out a larger smart-home ecosystem , with several devices coming later this year as part of its Apple Home Collection, including indoor and outdoor cameras, a smart thermostat, a video doorbell, a smart lock, and a couple of sensors. You can already control any Apple Home–compatible device on the HomeView, though, without needing Apple's lineup to release. The HomeView provides a similar experience to other smart displays , with a page you can swipe to for accessing all of the devices set up through your Apple Home app. It's easy to see the devices and quickly control them. Apple Home's biggest issue, though, continues to be compatibility. Many smart devices are only Amazon- and Google-compatible, though Matter is fixing some of that issue; I was able to connect the Ikea Varmblixt ($100) smart lamp to my Apple Home app thanks to the Matter compatibility. It was fast and seamless to control once set up, both over voice and touch. You can also touch to access your texts and FaceTime your contacts with the HomeView, which has been a pretty smooth experience for me. What's most interesting, though, is how the HomeView will verify that it's only you looking at your text messages. If it sees that someone else in your family is trying to look at or access your texts, it'll prompt that family member to switch over to their own account. It only works if they're alone in range of the device's camera, though; if they're peeking over your shoulder, access won't be denied. Apple isn't using FaceID for this, surprisingly enough. It uses biometric data to figure out who's asking via a protected part of the processor Apple calls the Secure Exclave . It's a new technology that's also on the Apple Watch ; we'll have to see how it pans out in real time. Of course, we can't talk about a smart display and speaker without talking about one of the key features: the speaker. Sound is a big part of the enjoyment from this device, and while I enjoyed the audio quality, I found it frustrating to voice-request a song. When I asked for music without prompting which app it should come from, Siri asked me if I'd like it to come from Books, TikTok, or Spotify. And when I would request a song on Spotify, Siri would say I needed to “unlock my device,” but didn't specify if that needed to happen on my iPhone or my HomeView. Or it would simply tell me there was a problem and tell me to try again. This is a huge bummer for my day-to-day use: I have a 4-year-old who loves making his own music requests and has gotten excellent at asking Google to play his latest favorite song (we're finally coming off of him requesting “Ghostbusters” and "This Is Halloween" on a daily basis). Ultimately, the easiest way to play music as a Spotify user was using the handoff feature. The HomeView has a proximity-sharing feature similar to when you tap two iPhones to AirDrop a photo or other information, and it was much, much easier to pull up a song on my iPhone and simply place it near the HomeView to send what I was listening to to the speaker. I did really like that experience, but I think Spotify users will prefer other smart speakers if music playback is a primary feature they’re looking for. The sound itself was pretty good; I was happy jamming from a range of music, whether an autumn lo-fi mix or “The Call of the Mountains,” by Eluveitie. My long-time favorite song, “Dark Blue,” by Jack's Mannequin, sounded as clear with its piano keys and background drums as it did back in 2007 when I first started listening to it. The HomeView’s audio comes from the cylinder-like base that's only about 3 inches wide, giving it a slimmer profile than most smart display bases and even just stand-alone small smart speakers (the Google Home Speaker is about 5 inches at its widest point, for comparison). Inside that base sit two full-range drivers, a down-firing woofer that promises Spatial Audio, and two force-canceling passive radiators to build out the sound. So, would I tell you to buy this? Only if you're a total Apple devotee who would use all of your preferred, Apple-run apps in tandem with the Apple HomeView. But it's really best if you're looking to invest in an Apple-run smart home (or already have one) and want a touchscreen to control it with. Or love FaceTiming so much you want an extra device for it. Otherwise, you'd be just as happy with cheaper smart displays or a simple smart speaker. Power up with unlimited access to WIRED . extraction.body: After I published my review of the HomeView, Apple’s first smart display, y’all still had a ton of questions about how it works as a smart speaker. So, I spent a bunch more time testing its audio capabilities and support for third-party music apps — and found a few more frustrations along the way. Here are the answers to all your burning questions. The HomeView isn’t a replacement for a Sonos One, a full-size HomePod, or a similar-size speaker. In size and sound, the HomeView is closer to the HomePod Mini. I tested it alongside the Mini 2 (which sounds marginally better than the first-gen Mini) and found the tabletop HomeView mostly comparable, with these caveats: The HomeView has better bass and is slightly louder, but it’s not as clear and is less room-filling. You can hear them both in action in this video, alongside the full-size HomePod, the Sonos One, and the wall-mounted HomeView: [Video: Apple HomeView Smart Speaker Audio Testing] The difference comes down to the hardware. The Mini 2 has a single full-range driver and two passive radiators, whereas the tabletop HomeView has two drivers in the display, plus a woofer and two passive radiators in its base. While the woofer adds some oomph, the HomeView’s display, which sits over the speaker base, partly covers it, affecting the sound compared to the Mini. Apple added an accelerometer to the display because tilting it changes the sound, so HomeView adjusts its EQ in real time based on the angle. Still, the Mini, while not as loud, fills a room better, thanks partly to its 360-degree sound. (The HomeView supports Spatial Audio with Dolby Atmos, which the Mini 2 doesn’t.) The wall-mounted HomeView has only two drivers, with computational audio Apple says is “tuned specifically for on-wall placement.” It sounds fine but is noticeably thinner than the tabletop version, and bass is basically non-existent. I wouldn’t recommend it for its sound quality, but it’s great for talking to a visitor through your video doorbell. Can you pair two HomeViews for stereo sound? [Image: Two HomeViews can’t be paired for stereo sound, as the HomePod Minis can. While you can group HomeViews with any other AirPlay speakers to play music out of them all at once, you can’t pair two for a stereo setup or pair a HomeView with a HomePod or Mini. I like the sound of two Minis paired in stereo and use this setup in my office and my bedroom. They also work as speakers for my Apple TVs in those rooms. If you have $300 to spend on a good-sounding smart speaker setup, go with two Minis over a HomeView. I cover its uses extensively in my full review, but for audio in particular, I like that the screen acts like a jukebox, making it easy to change songs, select new music, and scroll through your podcasts or audiobooks — without needing to find a quarter! You can AirPlay to the HomeView as with any other AirPlay speaker, and audio handoff works the same as it does on HomePods. Tap your phone to the HomeView, and whatever is playing transfers to the speakers and the screen. Handoff also works in reverse, letting you send any content back to your phone. YouTube and YouTube TV videos also handed off, even though they don’t have an app on the HomeView. But Netflix and Amazon Prime Video only played audio, though both played video in the Safari browser. As with HomePods, if you’re holding your phone within a few inches, the HomeView will try to hand off content. However, you can play audio to any AirPlay speaker or group of speakers. I tested this on HomePods, Sonos speakers, and a Samsung TV, and it worked smoothly. For native apps (Apple Music, Podcasts, and Safari), the HomeView remembers the last speaker or speaker pair you used and automatically plays content through those when you return. Things get messier with third-party audio apps such as Spotify and Audible, and with Apple apps that use the CarPlay interface, such as Apple News and Apple TV. The HomeView only automatically uses the last speakers if you choose content from the HomeView screen. If you use Siri voice control, it defaults to the HomeView speaker. So, “Hey Siri, play ‘Femininomenon’ by Chappell Roan from Spotify” played music from HomeView’s speaker and not the stereo pair of Minis in my office, where I’d last been listening to Spotify. I could direct it to play music there by adding “on Office,” but that’s more of a mouthful than just “Hey Siri, play ‘Femininomenon’ by Chappell Roan,” which is all you need to say if you use Apple Music. Which brings me to another one of your most-asked questions — and my biggest complaint about this device as a smart speaker: How does it support third-party audio apps? Apple has taken a shortcut here: Rather than building a dedicated HomeView experience for app developers, the HomeView uses Apple’s existing CarPlay platform. This makes it easier for developers to put their apps on the HomeView — if an audio or video app supports CarPlay, it already works on the HomeView (there’s no support for other types of CarPlay apps). In practice, this creates frustrating limitations, including no search function and the need for a user profile on the HomeView and your phone on the same Wi-Fi.

I tested it alongside the Mini 2 (which sounds marginally better than the first-gen Mini) and found the tabletop HomeView mostly comparable, with these caveats: The HomeView has better bass and is slightly louder, but it’s not as clear and is less room-filling.

You can hear them both in action in this video, alongside the full-size HomePod, the Sonos One, and the wall-mounted HomeView: [Video: Apple HomeView Smart Speaker Audio Testing] The difference comes down to the hardware.
The Mini 2 has a single full-range driver and two passive radiators, whereas the tabletop HomeView has two drivers in the display, plus a woofer and two passive radiators in its base.
While the woofer adds some oomph, the HomeView’s display, which sits over the speaker base, partly covers it, affecting the sound compared to the Mini.
Apple added an accelerometer to the display because tilting it changes the sound, so HomeView adjusts its EQ in real time based on the angle.

Still, the Mini, while not as loud, fills a room better, thanks partly to its 360-degree sound. (The HomeView supports Spatial Audio with Dolby Atmos, which the Mini 2 doesn’t.) The wall-mounted HomeView has only two drivers, with computational audio Apple says is “tuned specifically for on-wall placement.” It sounds fine but is noticeably thinner than the tabletop version, and bass is basically non-existent.
I wouldn’t recommend it for its sound quality, but it’s great for talking to a visitor through your video doorbell.
Can you pair two HomeViews for stereo sound? [Image: Two HomeViews can’t be paired for stereo sound, as the HomePod Minis can.
While you can group HomeViews with any other AirPlay speakers to play music out of them all at once, you can’t pair two for a stereo setup or pair a HomeView with a HomePod or Mini.
I like the sound of two Minis paired in stereo and use this setup in my office and my bedroom.
They also work as speakers for my Apple TVs in those rooms.
If you have $300 to spend on a good-sounding smart speaker setup, go with two Minis over a HomeView.

I cover its uses extensively in my full review, but for audio in particular, I like that the screen acts like a jukebox, making it easy to change songs, select new music, and scroll through your podcasts or audiobooks — without needing to find a quarter!
You can AirPlay to the HomeView as with any other AirPlay speaker, and audio handoff works the same as it does on HomePods.
Tap your phone to the HomeView, and whatever is playing transfers to the speakers and the screen.
Handoff also works in reverse, letting you send any content back to your phone.
YouTube and YouTube TV videos also handed off, even though they don’t have an app on the HomeView.
But Netflix and Amazon Prime Video only played audio, though both played video in the Safari browser.
As with HomePods, if you’re holding your phone within a few inches, the HomeView will try to hand off content.
However, you can play audio to any AirPlay speaker or group of speakers.
I tested this on HomePods, Sonos speakers, and a Samsung TV, and it worked smoothly.
For native apps (Apple Music, Podcasts, and Safari), the HomeView remembers the last speaker or speaker pair you used and automatically plays content through those when you return.
Things get messier with third-party audio apps such as Spotify and Audible, and with Apple apps that use the CarPlay interface, such as Apple News and Apple TV.
The HomeView only automatically uses the last speakers if you choose content from the HomeView screen.
If you use Siri voice control, it defaults to the HomeView speaker.
So, “Hey Siri, play ‘Femininomenon’ by Chappell Roan from Spotify” played music from HomeView’s speaker and not the stereo pair of Minis in my office, where I’d last been listening to Spotify.

I could direct it to play music there by adding “on Office,” but that’s more of a mouthful than just “Hey Siri, play ‘Femininomenon’ by Chappell Roan,” which is all you need to say if you use Apple Music.
Which brings me to another one of your most-asked questions — and my biggest complaint about this device as a smart speaker: How does it support third-party audio apps?
Apple has taken a shortcut here: Rather than building a dedicated HomeView experience for app developers, the HomeView uses Apple’s existing CarPlay platform.

This makes it easier for developers to put their apps on the HomeView — if an audio or video app supports CarPlay, it already works on the HomeView (there’s no support for other types of CarPlay apps).
In practice, this creates frustrating limitations, including no search function and the need for a user profile on the HomeView and your phone on the same Wi-Fi.

extraction.body: In recent years, people have been increasingly looking for new ways to form platonic connections, as loneliness and social isolation have become more prevalent. In 2023, the U.S. Surgeon General went so far as to label this issue a public health crisis. Remote workers, who miss the everyday interactions found in an office, and younger individuals eager to create their adult social circles based on shared interests and hobbies, are among those seeking meaningful friendships. Thanks to online dating apps, the stigma associated with finding connections online has largely faded away. This has welcomed a new wave of apps focused on fostering friendships and building local communities. According to estimates from Appfigures, over a dozen local-focused friendship apps have collectively generated approximately $16 million in consumer spending in the U.S. so far this year. Some notable examples include Timeleft, Meet5, and Bumble's BFF. Additionally, these apps have garnered approximately 4.3 million downloads thus far in 2025. The apps aim to provide a less awkward solution than, for instance, approaching a stranger at the gym or local café and trying to strike up a conversation. These platforms clearly indicate that everyone using the app is looking for the same thing — friendship, not romance — making it much less intimidating to initiate conversations. From major players like Meetup to newer ones like 222, there are plenty of apps that cater to the growing demand for meaningful friendships. We've compiled a list of them for you to try out. Clyx is another emerging app in the group-based social networking landscape, with a strong focus on discovering local events. The social platform helps users find community events by integrating data from platforms like Ticketmaster and TikTok. Additionally, Clyx allows users to upload their contact lists, helping them see which events their friends plan to attend. The app also includes a feature that recommends other users to connect with at these events. As of now, Clyx operates exclusively in two cities: Miami and London. However, it has plans to expand to additional areas in the near future, with New York City and São Paulo at the top of the list. The app is available on the App Store and Google Play Store . Crowdier is a new group social app that lets friend groups connect with others. Users can create a group of 2-5 friends and browse other groups to arrange hangouts in person. To initiate a match, users can "Wave" at groups they like, and if those groups wave back, they can plan in a shared chat. A match requires the majority of both groups to agree. For example, 2 people in a 4-person group needs to say yes. Available on iOS and Android , Les Amís serves cities across Europe, including Amsterdam, Barcelona, Berlin, Madrid, Paris, and Stockholm. In the U.S., the app is available in Austin and New York, with plans to expand to Boston, Miami, and Los Angeles. The app uses a paid membership model that varies by city, with fees of $70 in New York and €55 in Amsterdam. This European community-building app recently launched in the U.S., targeting users over 40 who want to meet new people in their area and participate in group activities such as picnics, concerts, and hiking. Notably, in a short time, there have been around 777,000 U.S. downloads so far across the App Store and Google Play Store , according to Appfigures estimates. Pie is another one of the newer social apps on the market. It features an AI-driven quiz designed to predict which users are most likely to be compatible with each other. Each person who RSVPs to a Pie event takes a brief personality assessment, and the algorithm organizes attendees into groups of six, who are then added to a group chat within the Pie app, allowing them to interact with each other before the event. Currently, the app is only available in Austin, Chicago, and San Francisco. Users can download Pie from the App Store and Google Play Store . Washed Up is a social event discovery app that launched in early 2026, designed for people in the Los Angeles area who want an easier way to find things to do and meet new people. The app helps users discover local events, such as concerts, trivia nights, and comedy shows, while also giving them a built-in way to connect with others who plan to attend. Instead of going to events alone, users can create or join "plans," which are small group meetups tied to specific events. Users can browse these plans and request to join, chat with the group, and add new friends, making it easier to show up to events with people rather than by themselves. It's available to download on the App Store . Wyzr Friends is an activity-based friendship app designed for adults 40 and older, catering to empty nesters, those who are divorced, and other users seeking to connect with like-minded individuals. Users can thumbs up or down potential friends and arrange in-person activities based on shared interests, such as going to the movies or hiking. It's available on iOS and Android devices in the U.S., Canada, Australia, Ireland, the Philippines, Singapore, and Mexico. Image Credits: Mmotion (Image has been modified) Mmotion is a newly launched friendship app that blends location tracking with social discovery to help users connect with people nearby and explore new bars and restaurants in their area. Upon joining, users can participate in interest-based groups — such as hiking, basketball, or art — view a map of active users, and send messages to those nearby. The app also highlights new places on the map, making it easy to find a restaurant or venue to try. Mmotion is currently only available to users in New York City on iOS and Android devices. Users must first submit an application to be considered. Launched in March 2026, Synchrony is a new social app tailored for neurodivergent adults. Founded by a mother of a son on the autism spectrum, it aims to create a supportive community through features like interest-based matching and two-step identity verification. This ensures that users engage safely, as both a user and a trusted person must verify personal details and a photo ID during registration. A standout feature is Jesse, an optional AI communication tool that assists users in navigating conversations. The AI provides editable prompts to help express thoughts, clarifies conversations, and offers boundary-setting suggestions. While the incorporation of AI may raise concerns, there are guardrails built into Jesse, such as avoiding medical advice. Here's what you need to know about how to spit-roast your beef. Hot take: A thank-you text is actually more than enough. The turkey can take its time. This somewhat obscure Southern buffet chain outranked some of the more well-known buffets around the U.S. with its homestyle comfort food and wide selection.

extraction.body: In today's world, where technology dominates, and many of us work from home, finding opportunities to meet new people and make friends can feel like a daunting task. Gone are the days when friendships were easily forged in office hallways or local community events. Now, as we navigate this digital age, most of us wonder how we connect with others outside of our immediate circles. Thankfully, the very technology that has made traditional ways of socializing less common also offers a solution. A variety of apps have been designed specifically to bridge the gap between wanting to make new friends and actually doing so. These platforms provide unique ways to meet like-minded individuals, whether you're looking for someone to explore new hobbies with, seeking support during life's ups and downs, or simply hoping to expand your social circle. Below, we share the six best apps to help you meet new people and make friends. We downloaded, tested, and experienced these platforms firsthand. From connecting with neighbors to meeting fellow enthusiasts in specific hobbies, these apps promise to make the process of finding new friends easier and more accessible. As the name suggests, Meetup is an app that helps you meet new people with common interests and hobbies with a focus on fostering real, face-to-face connections. To get started, create a profile and pick your interests. Then, choose what you are looking for. It can be to make new friends, practice a hobby with others, build a professional network, or simply socialize. Meetup will now show you all the groups or communities near your area. Pick one or more to start socializing. You can also take a look at the upcoming events near your location and book a reservation. Adding friends (or connections, as it is called on the app) is a bit different on Meetup as you must attend a Meetup event for it. If you find someone you would like to stay in touch with, you can add them on the app. The potential connections show up for 24 hours after the event. You can find the app on both the Play Store and the App Store . Bumble BFF emerges from one of the popular dating apps , Bumble, but with a twist about forging platonic friendships. Like its dating counterpart, you create a profile, but this time, it's tailored to highlight what makes you a great friend. To get started, download the Bumble app and create an account. You can also link your Facebook or Instagram accounts to your profile. In the Choose a mode to get started window, select BFF. This will switch your profile from dating to friendship mode. You can now edit your profile by adding photos, a bio, and some basic information about yourself. You can also choose your preferences for your potential friends, such as gender, age range, and distance. Once you are all set, it is time to start swiping through other BFF profiles. If you see someone you want to be friends with, swipe right. If not, swipe left. You can also tap on their profile to see more details and photos. If you and another user both swipe right on each other, you'll form a match and be able to chat with each other. You can also send voice notes, GIFs, and stickers to make the conversation more fun. To switch to your dating profile, simply click on the three bars at the top-left corner and choose Date. It is available on the Google Play Store as well as the App Store. extraction.body: In recent years, people have been increasingly looking for new ways to form platonic connections, as loneliness and social isolation have become more prevalent. In 2023, the U.S. Surgeon General went so far as to label this issue a public health crisis. Remote workers, who miss the everyday interactions found in an office, and younger individuals eager to create their adult social circles based on shared interests and hobbies, are among those seeking meaningful friendships. Thanks to online dating apps, the stigma associated with finding connections online has largely faded away. This has welcomed a new wave of apps focused on fostering friendships and building local communities. According to estimates from Appfigures, over a dozen local-focused friendship apps have collectively generated approximately $16 million in consumer spending in the U.S. so far this year. Some notable examples include Timeleft, Meet5, and Bumble's BFF. Additionally, these apps have garnered approximately 4.3 million downloads thus far in 2025. The apps aim to provide a less awkward solution than, for instance, approaching a stranger at the gym or local café and trying to strike up a conversation. These platforms clearly indicate that everyone using the app is looking for the same thing — friendship, not romance — making it much less intimidating to initiate conversations. From major players like Meetup to newer ones like 222, there are plenty of apps that cater to the growing demand for meaningful friendships. We've compiled a list of them for you to try out. Clyx is another emerging app in the group-based social networking landscape, with a strong focus on discovering local events. The social platform helps users find community events by integrating data from platforms like Ticketmaster and TikTok. Additionally, Clyx allows users to upload their contact lists, helping them see which events their friends plan to attend. The app also includes a feature that recommends other users to connect with at these events. As of now, Clyx operates exclusively in two cities: Miami and London. However, it has plans to expand to additional areas in the near future, with New York City and São Paulo at the top of the list. The app is available on the App Store and Google Play Store . Crowdier is a new group social app that lets friend groups connect with others. Users can create a group of 2-5 friends and browse other groups to arrange hangouts in person. To initiate a match, users can "Wave" at groups they like, and if those groups wave back, they can plan in a shared chat. A match requires the majority of both groups to agree. For example, 2 people in a 4-person group needs to say yes. Available on iOS and Android , Les Amís serves cities across Europe, including Amsterdam, Barcelona, Berlin, Madrid, Paris, and Stockholm. In the U.S., the app is available in Austin and New York, with plans to expand to Boston, Miami, and Los Angeles. The app uses a paid membership model that varies by city, with fees of $70 in New York and €55 in Amsterdam. This European community-building app recently launched in the U.S., targeting users over 40 who want to meet new people in their area and participate in group activities such as picnics, concerts, and hiking. Notably, in a short time, there have been around 777,000 U.S. downloads so far across the App Store and Google Play Store , according to Appfigures estimates. Pie is another one of the newer social apps on the market. It features an AI-driven quiz designed to predict which users are most likely to be compatible with each other. Each person who RSVPs to a Pie event takes a brief personality assessment, and the algorithm organizes attendees into groups of six, who are then added to a group chat within the Pie app, allowing them to interact with each other before the event. Currently, the app is only available in Austin, Chicago, and San Francisco. Users can download Pie from the App Store and Google Play Store . Washed Up is a social event discovery app that launched in early 2026, designed for people in the Los Angeles area who want an easier way to find things to do and meet new people. The app helps users discover local events, such as concerts, trivia nights, and comedy shows, while also giving them a built-in way to connect with others who plan to attend. Instead of going to events alone, users can create or join "plans," which are small group meetups tied to specific events. Users can browse these plans and request to join, chat with the group, and add new friends, making it easier to show up to events with people rather than by themselves. It's available to download on the App Store . Wyzr Friends is an activity-based friendship app designed for adults 40 and older, catering to empty nesters, those who are divorced, and other users seeking to connect with like-minded individuals. Users can thumbs up or down potential friends and arrange in-person activities based on shared interests, such as going to the movies or hiking. Crowdier is a new group social app that lets friend groups connect with others. Users can create a group of 2-5 friends and browse other groups to arrange hangouts in person.

To initiate a match, users can “Wave” at groups they like, and if those groups wave back, they can plan in a shared chat. A match requires the majority of both groups to agree. For example, 2 people in a 4-person group needs to say yes.

Available on iOS and Android , Les Amís serves cities across Europe, including Amsterdam, Barcelona, Berlin, Madrid, Paris, and Stockholm. In the U.S., the app is available in Austin and New York, with plans to expand to Boston, Miami, and Los Angeles.
The app uses a paid membership model that varies by city, with fees of $70 in New York and €55 in Amsterdam.

The local event-discovery platform has been around since 2002, helping millions of users connect with others who share similar interests. Users can RSVP to events; join groups that cater to a variety of hobbies, professions, or social causes; and create their own groups and events. They can also chat with group members and post updates and photos from gatherings.

This European community-building app recently launched in the U.S., targeting users over 40 who want to meet new people in their area and participate in group activities such as picnics, concerts, and hiking. Notably, in a short time, there have been around 777,000 U.S. downloads so far across the App Store and Google Play Store , according to Appfigures estimates.

Pie is another one of the newer social apps on the market. It features an AI-driven quiz designed to predict which users are most likely to be compatible with each other. Each person who RSVPs to a Pie event takes a brief personality assessment, and the algorithm organizes attendees into groups of six, who are then added to a group chat within the Pie app, allowing them to interact with each other before the event.
Currently, the app is only available in Austin, Chicago, and San Francisco. Users can download Pie from the App Store and Google Play Store .

Users can book dinners online or through the app . In terms of pricing, it varies depending on the country and restaurant. Users pay for a ticket up front and are responsible for covering their own dinner and drinks.
Washed Up is a social event discovery app that launched in early 2026, designed for people in the Los Angeles area who want an easier way to find things to do and meet new people.

The app helps users discover local events, such as concerts, trivia nights, and comedy shows, while also giving them a built-in way to connect with others who plan to attend. Instead of going to events alone, users can create or join “plans,” which are small group meetups tied to specific events. Users can browse these plans and request to join, chat with the group, and add new friends, making it easier to show up to events with people rather than by themselves.
It’s available to download on the App Store .

Wyzr Friends is an activity-based friendship app designed for adults 40 and older, catering to empty nesters, those who are divorced, and other users seeking to connect with like-minded individuals. Users can thumbs up or down potential friends and arrange in-person activities based on shared interests, such as going to the movies or hiking.
It’s available on iOS and Android devices in the U.S., Canada, Australia, Ireland, the Philippines, Singapore, and Mexico.

Mmotion is a newly launched friendship app that blends location tracking with social discovery to help users connect with people nearby and explore new bars and restaurants in their area. Upon joining, users can participate in interest-based groups — such as hiking, basketball, or art — view a map of active users, and send messages to those nearby. The app also highlights new places on the map, making it easy to find a restaurant or venue to try.
Mmotion is currently only available to users in New York City on iOS and Android devices. Users must first submit an application to be considered.

Launched in March 2026, Synchrony is a new social app tailored for neurodivergent adults. Founded by a mother of a son on the autism spectrum, it aims to create a supportive community through features like interest-based matching and two-step identity verification. This ensures that users engage safely, as both a user and a trusted person must verify personal details and a photo ID during registration.

A standout feature is Jesse, an optional AI communication tool that assists users in navigating conversations. The AI provides editable prompts to help express thoughts, clarifies conversations, and offers boundary-setting suggestions. While the incorporation of AI may raise concerns, there are guardrails built into Jesse, such as avoiding medical advice.

extraction.body: In today's world, where technology dominates, and many of us work from home, finding opportunities to meet new people and make friends can feel like a daunting task. Gone are the days when friendships were easily forged in office hallways or local community events. Now, as we navigate this digital age, most of us wonder how we connect with others outside of our immediate circles. Thankfully, the very technology that has made traditional ways of socializing less common also offers a solution. A variety of apps have been designed specifically to bridge the gap between wanting to make new friends and actually doing so. These platforms provide unique ways to meet like-minded individuals, whether you're looking for someone to explore new hobbies with, seeking support during life's ups and downs, or simply hoping to expand your social circle. Below, we share the six best apps to help you meet new people and make friends. We downloaded, tested, and experienced these platforms firsthand. From connecting with neighbors to meeting fellow enthusiasts in specific hobbies, these apps promise to make the process of finding new friends easier and more accessible. As the name suggests, Meetup is an app that helps you meet new people with common interests and hobbies with a focus on fostering real, face-to-face connections. To get started, create a profile and pick your interests. Then, choose what you are looking for. It can be to make new friends, practice a hobby with others, build a professional network, or simply socialize. Meetup will now show you all the groups or communities near your area. Pick one or more to start socializing. You can also take a look at the upcoming events near your location and book a reservation. Adding friends (or connections, as it is called on the app) is a bit different on Meetup as you must attend a Meetup event for it. If you find someone you would like to stay in touch with, you can add them on the app. The potential connections show up for 24 hours after the event. You can find the app on both the Play Store and the App Store . Bumble BFF emerges from one of the popular dating apps , Bumble, but with a twist about forging platonic friendships. Like its dating counterpart, you create a profile, but this time, it's tailored to highlight what makes you a great friend. To get started, download the Bumble app and create an account. You can also link your Facebook or Instagram accounts to your profile. In the Choose a mode to get started window, select BFF. This will switch your profile from dating to friendship mode. You can now edit your profile by adding photos, a bio, and some basic information about yourself. You can also choose your preferences for your potential friends, such as gender, age range, and distance. Once you are all set, it is time to start swiping through other BFF profiles. If you see someone you want to be friends with, swipe right. If not, swipe left. You can also tap on their profile to see more details and photos. If you and another user both swipe right on each other, you'll form a match and be able to chat with each other. You can also send voice notes, GIFs, and stickers to make the conversation more fun. To switch to your dating profile, simply click on the three bars at the top-left corner and choose Date. It is available on the Google Play Store as well as the App Store. In an age where digital connections often replace face-to-face interactions, the sense of community in neighborhoods has seen a notable decline. You don't normally see neighbors catch up over backyard fences or community gatherings. However, this shift has left many longing for a sense of belonging and connection right where they live. The Nextdoor app is designed with exactly this in mind, as it is a private social network for you and your neighbors. Like popular social media platforms , Nextdoor also features a news feed where you can scroll through updates, share in the joys and concerns of your neighbors, and engage with the local chatter. You can even discover products and services offered by local businesses. To view a list of neighbors on the app, click the More button in the bottom pane. Tap on a neighbor's profile to see their bio, posts, and groups. You can also send them a private message, a compliment, or a friend request. You can download it from the Google Play Store or the App Store . LMK is another innovative app designed to make the process of making new friends as simple and engaging as possible. Standing for "Let Me Know," LMK lets you create stickers and poll your friends for honest answers. Once you have downloaded the app and created the account, you can start crafting your own stickers or selecting from a variety of pre-made options. These stickers can be anything from a simple question about what to wear to an event to more complex queries seeking advice on personal matters. You then share these stickers with your friends or the wider LMK community, inviting honest and anonymous feedback. This feature not only sparks conversations but also encourages a level of openness and sincerity often missing in traditional social media interactions. Since the platform emphasizes voice interactions instead of relying solely on text messages, you can also engage in voice chats if you wish to create a more personal and immediate connection with others. This is perfect for people who prefer speaking to typing and enjoy having conversations in real time. You can download it using both the Google Play Store and the App Store. Like Bumble BFF, MeetMe is an app that combines social networking and online dating. It allows you to meet new people who share your interests and want to chat, date, or go live. You can create a profile, browse through other users' profiles, and send messages for free. You can also play games, join groups, and watch live streams of other members. In addition to its interactive features, MeetMe incorporates a virtual currency system known as MeetMe credits. These credits add another layer of engagement to the app, allowing users to access premium features and enhance their visibility within the community. For instance, you can use credits to boost your profile, making it more likely to be seen by others, or to purchase virtual gifts you can send to friends or people you're interested in during live streams. One downside of the app is that it has a bit of a low-quality matching system that relies on your location and preferences. You can't filter your matches by more specific criteria, such as age, gender, or compatibility score. You also can't see much information about other users' profiles, which means you need to rely on their photos, bio, and messages to get to know them better. Additionally, MeetMe has a lot of ads and pop-ups that interrupt your experience and slow down the app. You can find it on both the Google Play Store and the App Store . Discord isn't typically the first name that comes to mind when you think of apps for making new friends, but it's surprisingly effective at connecting people with shared interests. This platform was originally designed for gamers to chat and organize play sessions but has now evolved into a social platform where communities across various interests come together. Whether you're into gaming, books, music, or even gardening, there's a good chance you'll find a Discord server that feels like home. At its core, Discord is built around servers, which are individual communities centered around specific themes or activities. Within these servers, you'll find various channels for text, voice, and video conversations, which allow you to engage in real-time discussions about topics they care about. To join a server, choose Servers from the bottom pane and tap on the plus icon. Pick a category of your interest, browse through the available servers, and join one. Upon joining a server, you can start engaging by introducing yourself in the welcome or general chat channel. Participation is key on Discord. Join ongoing discussions, contribute to topics you're knowledgeable about, or simply share memes and content you enjoy. Making friends on Discord often happens organically through these interactions. As you become more active within the community, you can start adding people as friends for one-on-one conversations. You can download it from the Google Play Store and the App Store . While the convenience of making new friends online is undeniable, it's important to approach these interactions with a level of caution. No matter if it's in your hometown or meeting people when traveling abroad , the digital world, for all its benefits, also carries risks such as misinformation, privacy concerns, and the potential for encountering individuals with malicious intent. Safety should always be a priority when navigating online friendships. To start, always protect your personal information. Be mindful of what you share in public profiles and conversations. It's wise to keep details like your address, phone number, and other sensitive information private until you've established a strong trust foundation with someone. When it comes to moving an online friendship into the real world, choosing a public place for your first meeting is crucial. Whether it's a coffee shop, a park, or a public event, meeting in an area where others are present provides an additional layer of safety for both parties. Additionally, listen to your instincts. If something feels off about a person or a situation, don't ignore those feelings. Finally, consider using the safety features provided by many social platforms. Features like blocking, reporting, and privacy settings help you safely manage your online interactions. Making new friends online can be a rewarding experience, but it's important to navigate these relationships carefully and thoughtfully to ensure a safe and positive experience for everyone involved.

passages: Thousands of flights have been delayed at Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport, the world's busiest airport, after a technical failure at Delta Air Lines disrupted operations and triggered delays across the United States.

The disruption comes as millions of Americans prepare to travel for Thanksgiving, one of the busiest periods on the US holiday calendar.

Delays there can have a knock-on effect across its wider network as aircraft and crew schedules are disrupted.
The restriction was later lifted and replaced with a ground delay programme, allowing flights to depart for the airport but requiring them to wait longer.

extraction.body: Thousands of flights have been delayed at Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport, the world's busiest airport, after a technical failure at Delta Air Lines disrupted operations and triggered delays across the United States. The disruption comes as millions of Americans prepare to travel for Thanksgiving, one of the busiest periods on the US holiday calendar. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) initially issued a ground stop for Delta flights heading to Atlanta, warning that more than 3,500 flights could be affected. The restriction was later lifted and replaced with a ground delay programme, allowing flights to depart for the airport but requiring them to wait longer. The programme, which began at around 08:40 local time, initially imposed average delays of 57 minutes, with some reaching 111 minutes. The delays were expected to remain in place until 12:59. By 11:00, 681 flights had been delayed at Atlanta airport, while 591 Delta flights were delayed across the country, according to flight-tracking service FlightAware. The problem was caused by a failure in Delta's automated system for calculating aircraft weight and balance, a critical process that must be completed before take-off. Delta said it had switched to manual procedures while engineers worked to restore the automated system. "Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation," the airline said in a statement. "We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism." The carrier also said it was working with air traffic control authorities to manage the disruption and prevent congestion at airport gates and on the tarmac at its Atlanta hub. The initial ground stop, which began at 07:46 local time, affected Delta mainline and subsidiary flights travelling to Atlanta from 14 of the 20 air traffic control centre areas across the contiguous United States. Although the restrictions were later eased, the disruption continued to affect flights across the country. Atlanta is Delta's primary hub, with nearly 1,000 departures on peak days to more than 200 destinations. Delays there can have a knock-on effect across its wider network as aircraft and crew schedules are disrupted. Hartsfield-Jackson retained its position as the world's busiest airport by passenger traffic in 2025, handling 106 million passengers. Weight-and-balance calculations are essential for flight safety. Airlines must account for the aircraft's weight, fuel, passengers, baggage and cargo to ensure that its total weight and centre of gravity remain within approved limits. The disruption comes at the start of the Thanksgiving travel rush. Airport officials expect more than four million passengers to pass through Hartsfield-Jackson between 19 November and 1 December, around 5% more than during the same period last year.

extraction.body: Thousands of flights have been delayed at Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport, the world's busiest airport, after a technical failure at Delta Air Lines disrupted operations and triggered delays across the United States. The disruption comes as millions of Americans prepare to travel for Thanksgiving, one of the busiest periods on the US holiday calendar. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) initially issued a ground stop for Delta flights heading to Atlanta, warning that more than 3,500 flights could be affected. The restriction was later lifted and replaced with a ground delay programme, allowing flights to depart for the airport but requiring them to wait longer. The programme, which began at around 08:40 local time, initially imposed average delays of 57 minutes, with some reaching 111 minutes. The delays were expected to remain in place until 12:59. By 11:00, 681 flights had been delayed at Atlanta airport, while 591 Delta flights were delayed across the country, according to flight-tracking service FlightAware. The problem was caused by a failure in Delta's automated system for calculating aircraft weight and balance, a critical process that must be completed before take-off. Delta said it had switched to manual procedures while engineers worked to restore the automated system. "Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation," the airline said in a statement. "We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism." The carrier also said it was working with air traffic control authorities to manage the disruption and prevent congestion at airport gates and on the tarmac at its Atlanta hub. The initial ground stop, which began at 07:46 local time, affected Delta mainline and subsidiary flights travelling to Atlanta from 14 of the 20 air traffic control centre areas across the contiguous United States. Although the restrictions were later eased, the disruption continued to affect flights across the country. Atlanta is Delta's primary hub, with nearly 1,000 departures on peak days to more than 200 destinations. Delays there can have a knock-on effect across its wider network as aircraft and crew schedules are disrupted. Hartsfield-Jackson retained its position as the world's busiest airport by passenger traffic in 2025, handling 106 million passengers. Weight-and-balance calculations are essential for flight safety. Airlines must account for the aircraft's weight, fuel, passengers, baggage and cargo to ensure that its total weight and centre of gravity remain within approved limits. The disruption comes at the start of the Thanksgiving travel rush. Airport officials expect more than four million passengers to pass through Hartsfield-Jackson between 19 November and 1 December, around 5% more than during the same period last year.

passages: ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — Delta Air Lines said its automated system for calculating departing flights’ weight and balance is working again after a technical issue contributed to widespread delays Sunday.
The latest delays also come days after a nationwide ground stop caused mass cancellations at the Atlanta airport.
Just before 3 p.m., nearly 1,000 flights in and out of Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport were delayed, according to FlightAware.
That figure includes flights across airlines, not just Delta.
A ground stop issued Sunday morning for Delta flights bound for Atlanta later became a ground delay, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
The ground delay was scheduled to remain in effect until at least 1 p.m., with affected flights delayed nearly an hour before departure.
The Atlanta-based airline said approximately 70% of its delays and cancellations reported by flight-tracking website FlightAware were connected to the automation issue.
Delta attributed the rest to inclement weather and resulting air traffic control programs in New York City and the Northeast.

Passengers reported delays online at airports across the country, including Atlanta, Newark, LaGuardia, Reagan National, Dulles, Boston, Baltimore, Miami, Minneapolis, Nashville, San Antonio and Birmingham.
Delta and Delta Connection had approximately 5,000 flights scheduled Sunday.
The airline said its teams are focused on completing the rest of the day’s schedule and that cancellations are a last resort.
Delta apologized to customers and said it is rebooking passengers on the next available itinerary and providing meals and hotel rooms when necessary.
Delta said the disruption was not connected to FAA air traffic systems.
Because flights took longer to depart, fewer gates were available for arriving aircraft, adding to the delays.
