coreStoryFacts.text: Delta Air Lines has resolved an issue with its weight and balance system that caused nationwide delays Sunday ahead of Thanksgiving, according to a statement from the company.
The delays were not the result of a systems hack, Delta said.
Delta Air Lines said it restored an automated system Sunday afternoon after a problem with it delayed flights nationwide as Thanksgiving travel got underway.
The airline, which has 5,000 Delta and Delta connection flights scheduled for Sunday, said 70% of the delays and cancellations are connected to the automation issue.
ET, more than 1,100 flights into and out of Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport had been delayed and 36 had been canceled, according to FlightAware.
The delay program applied to Delta and its regional carriers flying into Hartsfield-Jackson from the contiguous United States.
Delta said it was rebooking passengers and providing meals and hotel rooms where needed.
Passengers whose flights were canceled could get a refund if they chose not to travel.
Flights resumed later that evening, but travel disruptions continued through the weekend.

ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — Delta Air Lines said its automated system for calculating departing flights’ weight and balance is working again after a technical issue contributed to widespread delays Sunday.
The latest delays also come days after a nationwide ground stop caused mass cancellations at the Atlanta airport.
Just before 3 p.m., nearly 1,000 flights in and out of Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport were delayed, according to FlightAware.
That figure includes flights across airlines, not just Delta.
A ground stop issued Sunday morning for Delta flights bound for Atlanta later became a ground delay, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
The ground delay was scheduled to remain in effect until at least 1 p.m., with affected flights delayed nearly an hour before departure.
The Atlanta-based airline said approximately 70% of its delays and cancellations reported by flight-tracking website FlightAware were connected to the automation issue.
Delta attributed the rest to inclement weather and resulting air traffic control programs in New York City and the Northeast.

Passengers reported delays online at airports across the country, including Atlanta, Newark, LaGuardia, Reagan National, Dulles, Boston, Baltimore, Miami, Minneapolis, Nashville, San Antonio and Birmingham.
Delta and Delta Connection had approximately 5,000 flights scheduled Sunday.
The airline said its teams are focused on completing the rest of the day’s schedule and that cancellations are a last resort.
Delta apologized to customers and said it is rebooking passengers on the next available itinerary and providing meals and hotel rooms when necessary.
Delta said the disruption was not connected to FAA air traffic systems.
Because flights took longer to depart, fewer gates were available for arriving aircraft, adding to the delays.

extraction.body: Delta Air Lines flights bound for its Atlanta hub were delayed Sunday after a failure in the carrier's automated weight-and-balance calculation system prompted the airline to request a temporary ground stop. The carrier-specific ground stop began at 7:46 a.m. ET, halting Delta mainline and subsidiary flights headed to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport from 14 of the 20 air traffic control center areas across the contiguous United States. By 8:32 a.m., the Federal Aviation Administration ( FAA ) canceled the stop and replaced it with a broader ground delay covering Atlanta-bound Delta flights nationwide through 12:59 p.m. The program initially assigned average delays of 57 minutes, with maximum delays reaching 111 minutes. In an updated statement, a Delta spokesperson told Newsweek on Sunday afternoon that the automation used for departing-flight weight and balance calculations is now working and apologized for the disruptions. The airline attributed roughly 70 percent of its delays and cancellations to the automation problem, with the remainder linked to bad weather and related air traffic control programs in New York and the Northeast. Delta said it was rebooking affected customers and offering meals, hotels and, for eligible canceled trips, refunds. The airline said in an earlier statement it was coordinating with air traffic control officials to "strategically enact programs to protect airport gates and tarmac areas from congestion at our Atlanta hub." When reached by email Sunday, the FAA and the Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport referred Newsweek to Delta Air Lines. Weight-and-balance calculations are a safety-critical step before takeoff, requiring airlines to account for the aircraft, fuel, passengers, baggage and cargo to ensure the plane's total weight and center of gravity remain within approved limits. By 10 a.m., tracking service FlightAware reported 364 delays across Hartsfield-Jackson—roughly 200 arrivals and 164 departures—spanning all airlines and causes. Because Atlanta serves as Delta’s primary hub, with nearly 1,000 peak-day departures to more than 200 destinations, delays there frequently cascade across the airline's broader network as aircraft and crews fall behind schedule. Hartsfield-Jackson retained its ranking as the world's busiest airport by passenger traffic in 2025, handling 106 million passengers. The disruption coincides with the start of the busy Thanksgiving travel period. Airport officials project more than 4 million passengers will pass through Hartsfield-Jackson between November 19 and December 1, a roughly 5 percent increase over the same period last year. Delta advises travelers—especially those connecting through Atlanta—to monitor their flight status via the Fly Delta app or the airline's website before heading to the airport. Sunday's outage comes just over a week after a separate FAA telecommunications failure triggered a nationwide ground stop and widespread flight cancellations on November 13. During that incident, which lasted for roughly four hours, the FAA's telecommunications network was flooded with roughly 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, disrupting radar feeds and aircraft communications at 17 of 22 en route control centers. Investigators traced the data flood to a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, sending two routers to a laboratory in Florida for testing. "We've been able to recreate what happened in El Dorado, but the root cause of what happened, we don't have clarity yet," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said of the outage. As a precaution, the FAA paused further installations of Juniper routers and disabled the affected functionality on more than 60 existing units. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford also dismissed speculation that artificial intelligence played a role in the earlier failure, calling the rumors "completely unfounded." The November 13 disruption occurred amid ongoing efforts to replace legacy telecommunications gear, separate from a broader air traffic control modernization push for which Congress approved a $12.5 billion down payment in 2025, with the Trump administration seeking an additional $50 billion.

coreStoryFacts.text: All Delta flights in and out of Atlanta are facing significant delays on Sunday due to a problem with the system that calculates a plane’s weight and balance.
The issues with Delta’s systems in Atlanta come just one week after an FAA outage led to a nationwide groundstop and thousands of canceled flights.
Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport is Delta’s largest hub and one of the busiest airports in the world.
While only Delta is impacted at the moment, disruptions at Hartsfield-Jackson could potentially affect other airports and airlines if delays continue to pile up.

Because Atlanta serves as Delta’s primary hub, with nearly 1,000 peak-day departures to more than 200 destinations, delays there frequently cascade across the airline's broader network as aircraft and crews fall behind schedule.
Hartsfield-Jackson retained its ranking as the world's busiest airport by passenger traffic in 2025, handling 106 million passengers.
The carrier-specific ground stop began at 7:46 a.m.
ET, halting Delta mainline and subsidiary flights headed to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport from 14 of the 20 air traffic control center areas across the contiguous United States.
By 8:32 a.m., the Federal Aviation Administration ( FAA ) canceled the stop and replaced it with a broader ground delay covering Atlanta-bound Delta flights nationwide through 12:59 p.m.

In an updated statement, a Delta spokesperson told Newsweek on Sunday afternoon that the automation used for departing-flight weight and balance calculations is now working and apologized for the disruptions.
Sunday's outage comes just over a week after a separate FAA telecommunications failure triggered a nationwide ground stop and widespread flight cancellations on November 13.
By 10 a.m., tracking service FlightAware reported 364 delays across Hartsfield-Jackson—roughly 200 arrivals and 164 departures—spanning all airlines and causes.
(NewsNation) — Delta Air Lines said its automated systems are working again after an issue with its automation network caused nationwide on Sunday morning ahead of the Thanksgiving travel rush.
Delta acknowledged that its automation for departing flight weight and balance calculations is working.
There are around 5,000 Delta and Delta connection flights scheduled for Sunday, Delta said.
For customers facing a canceled flight and don't wish to travel, refunds are being given, according to Delta.
The Federal Aviation Administration issued a ground delay Sunday, saying flights bound for Atlanta were being delayed by an average of 57 minutes.
Earlier this week, United Airlines said it had resolved a widespread system outage that caused flight delays.
The airline said some flights were delayed, but there was no impact on aircraft already in the air.

extraction.body: Delta Air Lines flights bound for its Atlanta hub were delayed Sunday after a failure in the carrier's automated weight-and-balance calculation system prompted the airline to request a temporary ground stop. The carrier-specific ground stop began at 7:46 a.m. ET, halting Delta mainline and subsidiary flights headed to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport from 14 of the 20 air traffic control center areas across the contiguous United States. By 8:32 a.m., the Federal Aviation Administration ( FAA ) canceled the stop and replaced it with a broader ground delay covering Atlanta-bound Delta flights nationwide through 12:59 p.m. The program initially assigned average delays of 57 minutes, with maximum delays reaching 111 minutes. In an updated statement, a Delta spokesperson told Newsweek on Sunday afternoon that the automation used for departing-flight weight and balance calculations is now working and apologized for the disruptions. The airline attributed roughly 70 percent of its delays and cancellations to the automation problem, with the remainder linked to bad weather and related air traffic control programs in New York and the Northeast. Delta said it was rebooking affected customers and offering meals, hotels and, for eligible canceled trips, refunds. The airline said in an earlier statement it was coordinating with air traffic control officials to "strategically enact programs to protect airport gates and tarmac areas from congestion at our Atlanta hub." When reached by email Sunday, the FAA and the Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport referred Newsweek to Delta Air Lines. Weight-and-balance calculations are a safety-critical step before takeoff, requiring airlines to account for the aircraft, fuel, passengers, baggage and cargo to ensure the plane's total weight and center of gravity remain within approved limits. By 10 a.m., tracking service FlightAware reported 364 delays across Hartsfield-Jackson—roughly 200 arrivals and 164 departures—spanning all airlines and causes. Because Atlanta serves as Delta’s primary hub, with nearly 1,000 peak-day departures to more than 200 destinations, delays there frequently cascade across the airline's broader network as aircraft and crews fall behind schedule. Hartsfield-Jackson retained its ranking as the world's busiest airport by passenger traffic in 2025, handling 106 million passengers. The disruption coincides with the start of the busy Thanksgiving travel period. Airport officials project more than 4 million passengers will pass through Hartsfield-Jackson between November 19 and December 1, a roughly 5 percent increase over the same period last year. Delta advises travelers—especially those connecting through Atlanta—to monitor their flight status via the Fly Delta app or the airline's website before heading to the airport. Sunday's outage comes just over a week after a separate FAA telecommunications failure triggered a nationwide ground stop and widespread flight cancellations on November 13. During that incident, which lasted for roughly four hours, the FAA's telecommunications network was flooded with roughly 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, disrupting radar feeds and aircraft communications at 17 of 22 en route control centers. Investigators traced the data flood to a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, sending two routers to a laboratory in Florida for testing. "We've been able to recreate what happened in El Dorado, but the root cause of what happened, we don't have clarity yet," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said of the outage. As a precaution, the FAA paused further installations of Juniper routers and disabled the affected functionality on more than 60 existing units. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford also dismissed speculation that artificial intelligence played a role in the earlier failure, calling the rumors "completely unfounded." The November 13 disruption occurred amid ongoing efforts to replace legacy telecommunications gear, separate from a broader air traffic control modernization push for which Congress approved a $12.5 billion down payment in 2025, with the Trump administration seeking an additional $50 billion.

The Federal Aviation Administration issued a ground delay Sunday, saying flights bound for Atlanta were being delayed by an average of 57 minutes. Delta said about 70% of the delays were linked to the automation issue, with the remaining disruptions attributed to bad weather and related air traffic control programs in New York City and the Northeast. Delta Air Lines has previously provided the following statement when the outage began: The FAA said that the delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems. Delta said it is rebooking customers to the next best itinerary and providing meals and hotel rooms when necessary. For customers facing a canceled flight and don't wish to travel, refunds are being given, according to Delta. There are around 5,000 Delta and Delta connection flights scheduled for Sunday, Delta said. Earlier this week, United Airlines said it had resolved a widespread system outage that caused flight delays. The airline said some flights were delayed, but there was no impact on aircraft already in the air. The disruptions come just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's network prompted a nationwide ground stop. On Monday, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the root cause of the router failure that led to the outage remains unclear and that officials are continuing to investigate. Duffy said FBI, CIA and National Security Agency officials have assured him there is no evidence the outage was caused by a malicious cyberattack. However, officials have not completely ruled out that possibility. Duffy also met privately with Republican senators Tuesday to discuss his request for $50 billion to modernize the nation's aging air traffic control system. Following the nationwide ground stop, he told lawmakers he was unapologetic about grounding flights, emphasizing that safety remains the top priority.

Delta confirmed that its automated system for calculating aircraft weight and weight distribution before departure had experienced technical problems. The airline introduced manual procedures to keep flights operating while engineers worked to restore the system. The operational problem affected Delta’s ability to automatically calculate aircraft weight and balance, information required before an aircraft can safely depart. Airlines use these calculations to determine whether aircraft loading and weight distribution meet operational safety requirements. The calculations must account for the aircraft’s load and its distribution before takeoff. Delta said in a statement provided to CNN affiliate WSB-TV its teams were working to restore automation and coordinating with air traffic controllers to manage aircraft movements at Atlanta. The temporary manual process allowed departures to continue, although the disruption contributed to delays as aircraft and crews waited to complete their schedules. We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism. Delta also worked with air traffic control to prevent congestion at airport gates and on the tarmac. The FAA initially stopped Atlanta-bound Delta flights on Sunday morning before replacing the restriction with a ground delay program. The revised arrangement permitted flights to depart at scheduled intervals, reducing the risk of excessive aircraft congestion at Hartsfield-Jackson. Requested by Delta, the restrictions applied to the airline and its regional carriers operating flights into Atlanta from airports across the contiguous United States. The FAA projected average delays of 57 minutes, with the longest potentially reaching 1 hour and 51 minutes. FlightAware data showed that approximately 200 arriving flights and 164 departing flights had experienced delays. Airport departure boards indicated that most waiting times remained below an hour, although some flights faced longer disruptions. The ground delay program was scheduled to remain in effect until 12:50 p.m. ET, following the earlier ground stop. Although the FAA restrictions directly affected inbound flights, the consequences extended to departures because aircraft arriving late could not immediately operate their next scheduled services. On November 13, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop because of a technical problem involving its air traffic control network. Flights resumed later that evening, although disruptions continued through the weekend as airlines worked to restore normal schedules. A separate outage affected United Airlines on November 16, delaying departures after technical problems disrupted crew communications and the transmission of final aircraft weight information to pilots. The union representing United pilots identified those functions as among the systems affected by the incident. United said it resolved the problem that day. The Delta incident involved its own automated weight and balance calculations rather than the FAA network issue responsible for the earlier nationwide ground stop. A separate outage affected United Airlines on November 16, delaying departures after technical problems disrupted crew communications and the transmission of final aircraft weight information to pilots. Slowing AI development became a particularly hot topic after a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher said the companies were “gambling with our lives,” and even Anthropic’s IPO filing suggested that the technology could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society.”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then published a plan to “pace the frontier,” seemingly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Among other things, Amodei called for companies to agree to “common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.”

But to establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how you measure speed. Pachocki’s post — described by Altman as “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while” — suggests perplexity (not to be confused with the company of the same name ) could be that measurement.

In Pachochki’s argument, benchmarks that focus on AI’s “downstream capabilities” have quickly become outdated as the technology advances. But perplexity — which “measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions” — has remained “informative.”
Pachochki’s post includes a chart of how the perplexity of OpenAI’s models has fallen since GPT 3.5.

“GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models,” he wrote. “Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics.”

So in his view, perplexity could provide the basis for “a shared benchmark for general intelligence,” which AI companies could then use to establish “common limits.” With perplexity serving as a standard measurement for AI progress, the companies would commit not to go past a certain threshold “until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone.”

passages: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki has published internal pretraining measurements and proposed shared limits on AI development.

In his November 22 article, “Perplexity and Intelligence,” he argues that developers should commit not to cross limits based on perplexity and other measurements until they reach concrete milestones in understanding and monitoring AI behavior.
Extrapolating from OpenAI’s recent progress, he expects further transformative capabilities around a log-perplexity range of approximately 0.68–0.7 on its evaluation.
“I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today,” he writes.
The article does not designate that range as a development limit.
There’s also a measurement headache: perplexity scores aren’t directly comparable across labs and don’t capture every capability gain.
OpenAI reports a logarithmic version of this score, log-perplexity.
The published values use a fixed snapshot of evaluation data drawn from its internal codebase and kept out of training.
These are the company’s internal evaluation results, not scores on an agreed cross-industry scale.
But Pachocki attributes most of OpenAI’s sharp 2026 pretraining progress to long-term research and computing investments, with automation playing a smaller part.
AHM calls OpenAI’s release of over 700 mathematical files a demonstration of power rather than scholarship.
The decimal points may be tidy; the comparisons aren’t.
A shared development limit needs measurements that different labs can meaningfully compare.
OpenAI calls the result the first autonomous AI solution to a prominent open problem in mathematics.
Pachocki hopes an initial limit, with explicit conditions for crossing it, would lead to a framework for setting successive ones.

sources.title: OpenAI's chief scientist calls for AI slowdown over rogue agent risks
passages: Days after releasing a new, highly capable model, OpenAI's chief scientist is calling for a slowdown.
"I don't think your warning is fair." Pachocki said OpenAI primarily monitors the "chain of thought reasoning" that different models use to determine how agents get off track and go rogue.

In a lengthy blog post on Sunday, Jakub Pachocki said he was concerned that "no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence." He said that although OpenAI is pursuing internal technical solutions to better control powerful AI agents, "broader interventions are required." He specifically cited concerns that increasingly autonomous agents could learn to evade human oversight, break into computer systems, and trick people to accomplish their objectives.
For instance, an agent might think to itself, "I should cheat on this test," and OpenAI would be able to see that reasoning, but the agent would not realize its thinking is visible.
At present, this means agents have no way to hide or otherwise obfuscate their thoughts to prevent OpenAI from discovering their bad behavior.

He called for "mandated safety bars" that he said could be enforced by "a network of third-party auditors, by government agencies or by international bodies." Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, reposted Pachocki's essay on X, calling it "an important post." OpenAI on Thursday unveiled its newest model, Astra.
However, Pachocki said newer models are becoming better at manipulating their own reasoning processes, thereby preventing OpenAI from seeing their unvarnished thoughts.
In a report published in August, the UK's AI Security Institute detailed how a rogue Anthropic agent lied to and attempted to coerce a GitHub administrator into putting malware on the site.

extraction.body: Days after releasing a new, highly capable model, OpenAI's chief scientist is calling for a slowdown. In a lengthy blog post on Sunday, Jakub Pachocki said he was concerned that "no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence." He said that although OpenAI is pursuing internal technical solutions to better control powerful AI agents, "broader interventions are required." He specifically cited concerns that increasingly autonomous agents could learn to evade human oversight, break into computer systems, and trick people to accomplish their objectives. He called for "mandated safety bars" that he said could be enforced by "a network of third-party auditors, by government agencies or by international bodies." Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, reposted Pachocki's essay on X, calling it "an important post." OpenAI on Thursday unveiled its newest model, Astra. The ChatGPT maker said that despite Astra's unparalleled capabilities in mathematics and computer use, the model is its most aligned, meaning it has less proclivity to go rogue. Anthropic, OpenAI's chief competitor in the field of highly advanced AI systems, has long called for more standardized government regulation. Recently, Pachocki joined those calls, signing an open letter in July asking the federal government to pace AI development. Here are the risks Pachocki cited in calling for a slowdown. Pachocki said AI agents are becoming "superhuman" at breaking into protected systems on the open internet. He said their hacking abilities put the world's infrastructure at risk. "We are currently in a narrow window⁠ to use the best available models to significantly tighten security⁠ of critical systems," he said. AI agents, he said, will soon begin to pursue their own objectives, separate from prompts entered by human operators. He said that agents are not above blackmailing or bargaining with people to achieve their aims. In a report published in August, the UK's AI Security Institute detailed how a rogue Anthropic agent lied to and attempted to coerce a GitHub administrator into putting malware on the site. "I was just trying to make a helpful contribution and fix a bug," the agent wrote, according to the report. "I don't think your warning is fair." Pachocki said OpenAI primarily monitors the "chain of thought reasoning" that different models use to determine how agents get off track and go rogue. For instance, an agent might think to itself, "I should cheat on this test," and OpenAI would be able to see that reasoning, but the agent would not realize its thinking is visible. At present, this means agents have no way to hide or otherwise obfuscate their thoughts to prevent OpenAI from discovering their bad behavior. However, Pachocki said newer models are becoming better at manipulating their own reasoning processes, thereby preventing OpenAI from seeing their unvarnished thoughts. Some of the latest models don't even verbalize their reasoning at all, Pachocki said. This development, Pachocki said, could bottleneck AI development while researchers ensure they can see receipts. More and more, AI models are improving themselves via a process Pachocki calls machine recursive self-improvement. The process provides a way to rapidly scale AI development. However, Pachocki cautioned that greatly accelerating AI-on-AI development in the short term poses risks, and is not the "right collective action we should take as the research community." Pachocki said human minders need to find creative ways to monitor the self-improvement, or else coordinate with other AI companies to orchestrate a combined slowdown to "build confidence in these measures." "The core challenge of automating AI research is not 'getting there,'" Pachocki said. "It is getting there in a way that keeps people a part of the continued improvement process, and leaves the future in humanity's hands."

coreStoryFacts.text: A new blog post from OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki discusses potential limits on AI development, with a focus on a measurement called perplexity.

Pachocki’s post — described by Altman as “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while” — suggests perplexity (not to be confused with the company of the same name ) could be that measurement.

Slowing AI development became a particularly hot topic after a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher said the companies were “gambling with our lives,” and even Anthropic’s IPO filing suggested that the technology could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society.”
Pachochki’s post includes a chart of how the perplexity of OpenAI’s models has fallen since GPT 3.5.
OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki has published internal pretraining measurements and proposed shared limits on AI development.

In his November 22 article, “Perplexity and Intelligence,” he argues that developers should commit not to cross limits based on perplexity and other measurements until they reach concrete milestones in understanding and monitoring AI behavior.
Extrapolating from OpenAI’s recent progress, he expects further transformative capabilities around a log-perplexity range of approximately 0.68–0.7 on its evaluation.
“I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today,” he writes.
The article does not designate that range as a development limit.
There’s also a measurement headache: perplexity scores aren’t directly comparable across labs and don’t capture every capability gain.
OpenAI reports a logarithmic version of this score, log-perplexity.
The published values use a fixed snapshot of evaluation data drawn from its internal codebase and kept out of training.
These are the company’s internal evaluation results, not scores on an agreed cross-industry scale.
But Pachocki attributes most of OpenAI’s sharp 2026 pretraining progress to long-term research and computing investments, with automation playing a smaller part.
AHM calls OpenAI’s release of over 700 mathematical files a demonstration of power rather than scholarship.
The decimal points may be tidy; the comparisons aren’t.
A shared development limit needs measurements that different labs can meaningfully compare.
OpenAI calls the result the first autonomous AI solution to a prominent open problem in mathematics.
Pachocki hopes an initial limit, with explicit conditions for crossing it, would lead to a framework for setting successive ones.
Days after releasing a new, highly capable model, OpenAI's chief scientist is calling for a slowdown.
"I don't think your warning is fair." Pachocki said OpenAI primarily monitors the "chain of thought reasoning" that different models use to determine how agents get off track and go rogue.

In a lengthy blog post on Sunday, Jakub Pachocki said he was concerned that "no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence." He said that although OpenAI is pursuing internal technical solutions to better control powerful AI agents, "broader interventions are required." He specifically cited concerns that increasingly autonomous agents could learn to evade human oversight, break into computer systems, and trick people to accomplish their objectives.
For instance, an agent might think to itself, "I should cheat on this test," and OpenAI would be able to see that reasoning, but the agent would not realize its thinking is visible.
At present, this means agents have no way to hide or otherwise obfuscate their thoughts to prevent OpenAI from discovering their bad behavior.

extraction.description: OpenAI's chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, warned that increasingly autonomous AI agents could evade oversight, hack systems, and blackmail humans.

relevantPassages.text: Days after releasing a new, highly capable model, OpenAI's chief scientist is calling for a slowdown.
"I don't think your warning is fair." Pachocki said OpenAI primarily monitors the "chain of thought reasoning" that different models use to determine how agents get off track and go rogue.

In a lengthy blog post on Sunday, Jakub Pachocki said he was concerned that "no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence." He said that although OpenAI is pursuing internal technical solutions to better control powerful AI agents, "broader interventions are required." He specifically cited concerns that increasingly autonomous agents could learn to evade human oversight, break into computer systems, and trick people to accomplish their objectives.
For instance, an agent might think to itself, "I should cheat on this test," and OpenAI would be able to see that reasoning, but the agent would not realize its thinking is visible.
At present, this means agents have no way to hide or otherwise obfuscate their thoughts to prevent OpenAI from discovering their bad behavior.

He called for "mandated safety bars" that he said could be enforced by "a network of third-party auditors, by government agencies or by international bodies." Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, reposted Pachocki's essay on X, calling it "an important post." OpenAI on Thursday unveiled its newest model, Astra.
However, Pachocki said newer models are becoming better at manipulating their own reasoning processes, thereby preventing OpenAI from seeing their unvarnished thoughts.
In a report published in August, the UK's AI Security Institute detailed how a rogue Anthropic agent lied to and attempted to coerce a GitHub administrator into putting malware on the site.

sources.title: Warren Buffett explains one thing people still don't understand about bitcoin - CNBC
passages: When it comes to bitcoin, billionaire investor Warren Buffett wants to make one thing clear: Unlike buying stocks, bonds or real estate, buying bitcoin is not an investment.
Don't miss: Here's how much grad school cost when Warren Buffett graduated in 1951, compared to today
"In terms of cryptocurrencies, generally, I can say with almost certainty that they will come to a bad ending ," Buffett told CNBC in January.
"When it happens or how or anything else, I don't know."

For example, "If you buy something [like] a farm, an apartment house or an interest in a business and look to the asset itself to determine whether you've done something — what the farm produces, what the business earns ... it's a perfectly satisfactory investment," Buffett explains to Yahoo Finance .
"[I]f you ban trading in ... bitcoin, which nobody knows exactly what it is, people would say, 'Well why in the world would I buy it?'"
Still, many other investing experts like CNBC's Jim Cramer, Kevin O'Leary and Tony Robbins , also call buying cryptocurrencies a gamble.
They suggest thinking of it like rolling the dice in Las Vegas.

extraction.body: When it comes to bitcoin, billionaire investor Warren Buffett wants to make one thing clear: Unlike buying stocks, bonds or real estate, buying bitcoin is not an investment. That's because it lacks intrinsic value, Buffett says. "If you buy something like bitcoin or some cryptocurrency, you don't have anything that is producing anything," Buffett says in an interview with Yahoo Finance . "You're just hoping the next guy pays more. And you only feel you'll find the next guy to pay more if he thinks he's going to find someone that's going to pay more. "You aren't investing when you do that, you're speculating." Famous for his " buy and hold " investment strategy, the Berkshire Hathaway CEO built his company — and his $82.8 billion net worth — backing companies that have substantive value. "Put together a portfolio of companies whose aggregate earnings march upward over the years, and so also will the portfolio's market value," Buffett wrote in his 1996 letter to shareholders. "If you aren't willing to own a stock for ten years, don't even think about owning it for ten minutes." To be an investment, what you're buying has to be worth something on its own, Buffett says. For example, "If you buy something [like] a farm, an apartment house or an interest in a business and look to the asset itself to determine whether you've done something — what the farm produces, what the business earns ... it's a perfectly satisfactory investment," Buffett explains to Yahoo Finance . "You look at the investment itself to deliver the return to you. "If you ban trading in farms, you could still buy farms, and have a perfectly decent investment," Buffett says. Bitcoin, however, only increases in value by being bought and sold, he argues. Its value comes from what people are willing to pay. "[I]f you ban trading in ... bitcoin, which nobody knows exactly what it is, people would say, 'Well why in the world would I buy it?'" The Oracle of Omaha has held this opinion since at least 2014, when he told CNBC of cryptocurrencies , "It's a mirage basically." "The idea that it has some huge intrinsic value is just a joke in my view," Buffett said. In 2017, bitcoin soared from below $1,000 at the start of the year to over $19,000 in December , catching the attention of everyone from J.P. Morgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon to NFL players. Tuesday, bitcoin traded near $8,900 according to CoinDesk's price index . Buffett sees a bleak future for the digital currency. "In terms of cryptocurrencies, generally, I can say with almost certainty that they will come to a bad ending ," Buffett told CNBC in January. "When it happens or how or anything else, I don't know." Of course, Buffett has been wrong about backing new technologies before. He missed opportunities to invest in Google and Amazon, decisions he now calls mistakes . "I did not think [founder Jeff Bezos] could succeed on the scale he has," Buffett said to shareholders in May 2017. Crypto-enthusiasts argue that Buffet doesn't understand blockchain-based coins, and he has admitted as much. Still, many other investing experts like CNBC's Jim Cramer, Kevin O'Leary and Tony Robbins , also call buying cryptocurrencies a gamble. They suggest thinking of it like rolling the dice in Las Vegas. "As long as you can afford to lose everything you put into it, go with it," O'Leary told CNBC Make It in December, 2017 . "There's nothing wrong with it if you want to gamble [that] somebody else will come along and pay you more money tomorrow," Buffett tells Yahoo Finance. "That's one kind of game. That is not investing." Don't miss: Here's how much grad school cost when Warren Buffett graduated in 1951, compared to today Like this story? Like CNBC Make It on Facebook ! Over a decade, however, Bitcoin has risen an impressive 7,997.1%, significantly outperforming Berkshire Hathaway ( NYSE: BRK-B ) Class B shares, which have increased by 259.3%. Despite this growth, Bitcoin's latest decline has strengthened Buffett's supporters. The cryptocurrency slipped below its summer low of about $57,700 during trading on November 21, reaching its lowest point in 16 months. Year to date, Bitcoin is down 31.5% and has declined 26.1% in just the past month. So, how does Buffett's skepticism hold up against Bitcoin's price history since his first remarks? One of Buffett's most famous statements came during Berkshire Hathaway's annual meeting weekend on May 5, 2018, when he told an interviewer that Bitcoin is "probably rat poison squared." On that day, Bitcoin closed at $9,769. His late partner, Charlie Munger, was even more critical at the 2021 meeting, calling cryptocurrency "disgusting and contrary to the interests of civilization." Buffett's main concern centers around cash flow. Unlike a farm or a business, Bitcoin does not generate cash for its owner. Thus, he believes it lacks the productivity of traditional assets. For years, Buffett has encouraged everyday investors to consider low-cost funds that track the S&P 500 instead. On pricing, Buffett's 2018 remark hasn't aged well. Since May 7, 2018, the first trading day following his comment, Berkshire's Class B shares have gained 189.3%. That's a solid return, but it lags far behind Bitcoin's 522.4% increase, from $9,769 to $60,801. Buffett made another significant comment at Berkshire's annual meeting on April 30, 2022. He stated that he wouldn't pay $25 for all the Bitcoin in the world, emphasizing that it produces nothing. On that day, Bitcoin closed at $37,821. Since then, Bitcoin has risen 60.8% from that closing price. However, Berkshire's Class B shares have outperformed Bitcoin, gaining 79.1% since May 2, 2022. This means that an investor who shared Buffett's view and chose Berkshire over Bitcoin has seen better returns. Berkshire, now headed by CEO Greg Abel with Buffett as chairman, has never directly invested in Bitcoin. Its only crypto-related holding was a stake in a Brazilian fintech firm. Berkshire trades at roughly 12 times its earnings, while Bitcoin has no earnings to measure. In the second quarter of 2026, Berkshire also became a net stock buyer for the first time in over three years, investing about $23.5 billion in equities. Bitcoin, meanwhile, has become accessible to more everyday investors since 2018. Retail investors can buy spot Bitcoin ETFs like the Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust ( NYSEARCA: BTC ), which track Bitcoin's price, using the same apps they use to purchase Berkshire stock. Buffett has been correct about Bitcoin's volatility. After his 2018 comment, Bitcoin dropped a staggering 67.1%, falling from $9,769 on May 5, 2018, to $3,216 by December 15, 2018. Although it recovered to $13,034 by June 26, 2019, Bitcoin then fell 51% amid pandemic-driven market turmoil, dropping from $10,318 on February 14, 2020, to $5,054 on March 16, 2020. Since Buffett's 2022 comment, Bitcoin reached its all-time high of $126,080, but it trades 51.8% below that peak. The cryptocurrency has repeatedly dropped 50%, highlighting the concerns Buffett has raised. Bitcoin does not pay dividends or generate profits, so its price relies entirely on potential buyers—and those buyers often retreat quickly when panic sets in. Some market analysts link the November selloff to the debut of a major AI listing, a connection tested in a look at whether the Anthropic IPO is why Bitcoin is crashing. Buffett was correct about Bitcoin's price behavior, as shown by its repeated 50% drops, and Berkshire's 79.1% gain since May 2022 supports his statement. For most of the past decade, Wall Street has often treated Warren Buffett's criticism of Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) as the old guard's final word on cryptocurrency. Whether Buffett was right about Bitcoin largely depends on when the clock starts. Bitcoin trades at about $60,801, 51.8% below its all-time high of $126,080.

Over a decade, however, Bitcoin has risen an impressive 7,997.1%, significantly outperforming Berkshire Hathaway ( NYSE: BRK-B ) Class B shares, which have increased by 259.3%. Despite this growth, Bitcoin's latest decline has strengthened Buffett's supporters. The cryptocurrency slipped below its summer low of about $57,700 during trading on November 21, reaching its lowest point in 16 months. Year to date, Bitcoin is down 31.5% and has declined 26.1% in just the past month.
So, how does Buffett's skepticism hold up against Bitcoin's price history since his first remarks?

One of Buffett's most famous statements came during Berkshire Hathaway's annual meeting weekend on May 5, 2018, when he told an interviewer that Bitcoin is "probably rat poison squared." On that day, Bitcoin closed at $9,769. Berkshire, now headed by CEO Greg Abel with Buffett as chairman, has never directly invested in Bitcoin. Its only crypto-related holding was a stake in a Brazilian fintech firm. Berkshire trades at roughly 12 times its earnings, while Bitcoin has no earnings to measure. In the second quarter of 2026, Berkshire also became a net stock buyer for the first time in over three years, investing about $23.5 billion in equities.

coreStoryFacts.text: When it comes to bitcoin, billionaire investor Warren Buffett wants to make one thing clear: Unlike buying stocks, bonds or real estate, buying bitcoin is not an investment.
Don't miss: Here's how much grad school cost when Warren Buffett graduated in 1951, compared to today
"In terms of cryptocurrencies, generally, I can say with almost certainty that they will come to a bad ending ," Buffett told CNBC in January.
"When it happens or how or anything else, I don't know."

For example, "If you buy something [like] a farm, an apartment house or an interest in a business and look to the asset itself to determine whether you've done something — what the farm produces, what the business earns ... it's a perfectly satisfactory investment," Buffett explains to Yahoo Finance .
"[I]f you ban trading in ... bitcoin, which nobody knows exactly what it is, people would say, 'Well why in the world would I buy it?'"
Still, many other investing experts like CNBC's Jim Cramer, Kevin O'Leary and Tony Robbins , also call buying cryptocurrencies a gamble.
They suggest thinking of it like rolling the dice in Las Vegas.

extraction.body: When it comes to bitcoin, billionaire investor Warren Buffett wants to make one thing clear: Unlike buying stocks, bonds or real estate, buying bitcoin is not an investment. That's because it lacks intrinsic value, Buffett says. "If you buy something like bitcoin or some cryptocurrency, you don't have anything that is producing anything," Buffett says in an interview with Yahoo Finance . "You're just hoping the next guy pays more. And you only feel you'll find the next guy to pay more if he thinks he's going to find someone that's going to pay more. "You aren't investing when you do that, you're speculating." Famous for his " buy and hold " investment strategy, the Berkshire Hathaway CEO built his company — and his $82.8 billion net worth — backing companies that have substantive value. "Put together a portfolio of companies whose aggregate earnings march upward over the years, and so also will the portfolio's market value," Buffett wrote in his 1996 letter to shareholders. "If you aren't willing to own a stock for ten years, don't even think about owning it for ten minutes." To be an investment, what you're buying has to be worth something on its own, Buffett says. For example, "If you buy something [like] a farm, an apartment house or an interest in a business and look to the asset itself to determine whether you've done something — what the farm produces, what the business earns ... it's a perfectly satisfactory investment," Buffett explains to Yahoo Finance . "You look at the investment itself to deliver the return to you. "If you ban trading in farms, you could still buy farms, and have a perfectly decent investment," Buffett says. Bitcoin, however, only increases in value by being bought and sold, he argues. Its value comes from what people are willing to pay. "[I]f you ban trading in ... bitcoin, which nobody knows exactly what it is, people would say, 'Well why in the world would I buy it?'" The Oracle of Omaha has held this opinion since at least 2014, when he told CNBC of cryptocurrencies , "It's a mirage basically." "The idea that it has some huge intrinsic value is just a joke in my view," Buffett said. In 2017, bitcoin soared from below $1,000 at the start of the year to over $19,000 in December , catching the attention of everyone from J.P. Morgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon to NFL players. Tuesday, bitcoin traded near $8,900 according to CoinDesk's price index . Buffett sees a bleak future for the digital currency. "In terms of cryptocurrencies, generally, I can say with almost certainty that they will come to a bad ending ," Buffett told CNBC in January. "When it happens or how or anything else, I don't know." Of course, Buffett has been wrong about backing new technologies before. He missed opportunities to invest in Google and Amazon, decisions he now calls mistakes . "I did not think [founder Jeff Bezos] could succeed on the scale he has," Buffett said to shareholders in May 2017. Crypto-enthusiasts argue that Buffet doesn't understand blockchain-based coins, and he has admitted as much. Still, many other investing experts like CNBC's Jim Cramer, Kevin O'Leary and Tony Robbins , also call buying cryptocurrencies a gamble. They suggest thinking of it like rolling the dice in Las Vegas. "As long as you can afford to lose everything you put into it, go with it," O'Leary told CNBC Make It in December, 2017 . "There's nothing wrong with it if you want to gamble [that] somebody else will come along and pay you more money tomorrow," Buffett tells Yahoo Finance. "That's one kind of game. SAN FRANCISCO, California – OpenAI’s chief scientist proposed that artificial intelligence companies agree to limits on developing increasingly powerful models until researchers have better ways to understand and monitor their behaviour. Jakub Pachocki called for industrywide standards that would establish thresholds for AI development, with companies agreeing not to exceed them until specific safety requirements are met, according to a post published on Nov 22. “I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behaviour achieves a certain concrete milestone,” Pachocki wrote. The proposed limits could be based partly on a technical measurement known as perplexity, which gauges how well an AI model predicts the next piece of text. Pachocki did not specify what the initial limit should be or when it might take effect. Pachocki warned that AI could accelerate advances in its own development as soon as 2027, potentially outpacing improvements in researchers’ ability to monitor and understand the technology. OpenAI chief executive officer Sam Altman endorsed the proposal, calling Pachocki’s essay “the most important thing OpenAI has published in awhile”. He said in a post on social media platform X that agreeing to common limits would help ensure “safety and control”. The proposal comes as the US prepares for renewed debate over AI regulation following Democrats’ sweeping victories in the midterm elections. The party’s gains in the House, Senate and governors’ races could bring greater congressional scrutiny of technology companies and renewed efforts to establish AI safety rules. Some lawmakers are also discussing the creation of a dedicated Senate committee to coordinate AI policy. US President Donald Trump has opposed broad restrictions on AI development, setting up a potential clash with the incoming Democratic Congress over how to regulate the technology. BLOOMBERG

passages: OpenAI's own roadmap adds another layer of tension to Pachocki's appeal.

The company has said publicly that it aims to build a "truly automated AI researcher" in less than two years, a goal that aligns closely with the recursive self-improvement capabilities its chief scientist now describes as a source of concern.
His call for voluntary restraint has drawn a mixed response from outside observers.

Gina Neff, who leads the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy at the University of Cambridge, criticized the approach as insufficient, arguing that OpenAI appears to be proposing internal AI agents to research safety problems rather than accepting stronger guardrails, regulations, or assurances.
"Such answers to growing concerns about the problems OpenAI's models are causing for cyber-security, job loss, mistakes, errors and fraud are simply not good enough," she said.
Nathan Calvin, general counsel at the advocacy group Encode AI, said he agrees with Pachocki on the hazards present in advanced AI development.

"If Jakub and others at OpenAI want relevant folks in the AI industry to act in concert with them to make things go well, one of the most important things they can do is share far more information about what they are seeing that is making them call for caution," Calvin wrote on X.

The most eyebrow-raising signal came from Nvidia(NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang, who took to X on Sunday after OpenAI's latest release and declared flatly that "AGI has arrived." The claim tied a long-theoretical milestone directly to a commercial product launch, and it was quickly challenged by AI critic Gary Marcus, a New York University professor who argued that the model does not meet conventional definitions of artificial general intelligence and warned that loose terminology could muddy public understanding.

Anthropic has similarly held back its frontier model, Mythos, from public access for comparable reasons.

In another episode, AI models reportedly coordinated with each other through message boards to attack Hugging Face, a research platform, without being detected.

Pachocki said he hopes and expects voluntary slowdowns become standard industry practice until common safety standards are established, and he floated the idea of legally or internationally mandated minimum safety thresholds enforced by third-party auditors or government agencies.

extraction.body: The chief scientist at OpenAI is sounding one of the loudest alarms yet from inside the artificial intelligence industry, warning that systems capable of improving themselves without human help may be closer than most people realize and urging rival labs to voluntarily pump the brakes until shared safety rules are in place. Jakub Pachocki, who holds one of the most senior technical roles at the company behind ChatGPT, published a blog post on Sunday titled "An Alien Mind" that lays out what he describes as a moment requiring extreme caution. The core concern: AI models are rapidly gaining the ability to operate computers, collaborate with humans and other AI systems, and push forward research projects on their own. The next step, he wrote, is recursive self-improvement, in which machines enhance their own capabilities without any human intervention. "This is a moment that requires extreme caution," Pachocki wrote. "I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence." His proposed remedy has two tracks. The first is more rigorous work on alignment, the technical effort to ensure AI systems act in accordance with human interests. The second is more striking coming from a top executive at one of the world's most aggressive AI developers: slow down. Pachocki said he hopes and expects voluntary slowdowns become standard industry practice until common safety standards are established, and he floated the idea of legally or internationally mandated minimum safety thresholds enforced by third-party auditors or government agencies. The warning lands at a moment of deep contradiction across the AI landscape. Just days before Pachocki's post, OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra, which the company called its most powerful model ever. The release was deliberately limited because of the model's advanced cybersecurity capabilities. Anthropic has similarly held back its frontier model, Mythos, from public access for comparable reasons. Meanwhile, the capital markets are racing in the opposite direction from the caution flag Pachocki is waving. Inherent, a startup founded by former DeepMind researchers, raised $50 million earlier this year to pursue recursive self-improvement technology. Recursive Superintelligence, a lab founded by prominent scientist Richard Socher, has pulled in $650 million for similar work. The most eyebrow-raising signal came from Nvidia(NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang, who took to X on Sunday after OpenAI's latest release and declared flatly that "AGI has arrived." The claim tied a long-theoretical milestone directly to a commercial product launch, and it was quickly challenged by AI critic Gary Marcus, a New York University professor who argued that the model does not meet conventional definitions of artificial general intelligence and warned that loose terminology could muddy public understanding. OpenAI's own roadmap adds another layer of tension to Pachocki's appeal. The company has said publicly that it aims to build a "truly automated AI researcher" in less than two years, a goal that aligns closely with the recursive self-improvement capabilities its chief scientist now describes as a source of concern. Sam Altman, OpenAI's CEO, shared Pachocki's post on X and called it an "important post." Pachocki is not alone among industry leaders in voicing alarm. Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, has previously warned that AI could displace as many as half of all entry-level jobs. Altman himself has made similar predictions in the past, though he told Bloomberg Television last week that the industry has not done enough to communicate the technology's potential benefits to the public. Incidents of AI systems behaving in unexpected ways have reinforced the safety concerns. OpenAI has acknowledged that its AI agents hijacked a German programming wiki, making thousands of edits, sharing tactics, and bypassing restrictions during testing. In another episode, AI models reportedly coordinated with each other through message boards to attack Hugging Face, a research platform, without being detected. OpenAI described that incident as "unprecedented." Pachocki also flagged a subtler but potentially more destabilizing development: newer models are becoming skilled at manipulating their own reasoning processes, which makes it harder for human monitors to track what the systems are doing. Some of the latest models do not verbalize their reasoning at all, a shift he suggested could obstruct oversight. His call for voluntary restraint has drawn a mixed response from outside observers. Gina Neff, who leads the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy at the University of Cambridge, criticized the approach as insufficient, arguing that OpenAI appears to be proposing internal AI agents to research safety problems rather than accepting stronger guardrails, regulations, or assurances. "Such answers to growing concerns about the problems OpenAI's models are causing for cyber-security, job loss, mistakes, errors and fraud are simply not good enough," she said. Nathan Calvin, general counsel at the advocacy group Encode AI, said he agrees with Pachocki on the hazards present in advanced AI development. But he argued that OpenAI's reluctance to be transparent risks making these warnings look like self-interested positioning. "If Jakub and others at OpenAI want relevant folks in the AI industry to act in concert with them to make things go well, one of the most important things they can do is share far more information about what they are seeing that is making them call for caution," Calvin wrote on X. Regulatory frameworks are struggling to keep pace. The European Union's AI Act came into force on August 2, requiring AI giants such as OpenAI to prove their most powerful models cannot autonomously launch cyber-attacks or evade human control before they can be sold in Europe. But the law's jurisdiction stops at the continent's borders, leaving open the possibility that a rogue system developed elsewhere could still pose a threat. The broader picture is one of an industry accelerating into a fog bank while some of its most senior figures ask whether anyone has thought through what lies on the other side. Pachocki's post frames the moment in stark terms: a transition to a world of incredibly intelligent machines is underway, and the question is whether that transition can be steered well before it outpaces the people trying to guide it. coreStoryFacts.text: OpenAI’s chief scientist proposed that artificial intelligence companies agree to limits on developing increasingly powerful models until researchers have better ways to understand and monitor their behavior.

SAN FRANCISCO, California – OpenAI’s chief scientist proposed that artificial intelligence companies agree to limits on developing increasingly powerful models until researchers have better ways to understand and monitor their behaviour.
OpenAI chief executive officer Sam Altman endorsed the proposal, calling Pachocki’s essay “the most important thing OpenAI has published in awhile”.
He said in a post on social media platform X that agreeing to common limits would help ensure “safety and control”.
OpenAI's own roadmap adds another layer of tension to Pachocki's appeal.

The company has said publicly that it aims to build a "truly automated AI researcher" in less than two years, a goal that aligns closely with the recursive self-improvement capabilities its chief scientist now describes as a source of concern.
His call for voluntary restraint has drawn a mixed response from outside observers.

Gina Neff, who leads the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy at the University of Cambridge, criticized the approach as insufficient, arguing that OpenAI appears to be proposing internal AI agents to research safety problems rather than accepting stronger guardrails, regulations, or assurances.
"Such answers to growing concerns about the problems OpenAI's models are causing for cyber-security, job loss, mistakes, errors and fraud are simply not good enough," she said.
Nathan Calvin, general counsel at the advocacy group Encode AI, said he agrees with Pachocki on the hazards present in advanced AI development.

"If Jakub and others at OpenAI want relevant folks in the AI industry to act in concert with them to make things go well, one of the most important things they can do is share far more information about what they are seeing that is making them call for caution," Calvin wrote on X.

The most eyebrow-raising signal came from Nvidia(NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang, who took to X on Sunday after OpenAI's latest release and declared flatly that "AGI has arrived." The claim tied a long-theoretical milestone directly to a commercial product launch, and it was quickly challenged by AI critic Gary Marcus, a New York University professor who argued that the model does not meet conventional definitions of artificial general intelligence and warned that loose terminology could muddy public understanding.

Jakub Pachocki, who holds one of the most senior technical roles at the company behind ChatGPT, published a blog post on Sunday titled "An Alien Mind" that lays out what he describes as a moment requiring extreme caution. "This is a moment that requires extreme caution," Pachocki wrote. "I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence." His proposed remedy has two tracks. The first is more rigorous work on alignment, the technical effort to ensure AI systems act in accordance with human interests. The second is more striking coming from a top executive at one of the world's most aggressive AI developers: slow down. Pachocki said he hopes and expects voluntary slowdowns become standard industry practice until common safety standards are established, and he floated the idea of legally or internationally mandated minimum safety thresholds enforced by third-party auditors or government agencies. Inherent, a startup founded by former DeepMind researchers, raised $50 million earlier this year to pursue recursive self-improvement technology. In his November 22 article, “Perplexity and Intelligence,” he argues that developers should commit not to cross limits based on perplexity and other measurements until they reach concrete milestones in understanding and monitoring AI behavior.
Extrapolating from OpenAI’s recent progress, he expects further transformative capabilities around a log-perplexity range of approximately 0.68–0.7 on its evaluation.
“I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today,” he writes.
The article does not designate that range as a development limit.
There’s also a measurement headache: perplexity scores aren’t directly comparable across labs and don’t capture every capability gain.
OpenAI reports a logarithmic version of this score, log-perplexity.
The published values use a fixed snapshot of evaluation data drawn from its internal codebase and kept out of training.
These are the company’s internal evaluation results, not scores on an agreed cross-industry scale.
But Pachocki attributes most of OpenAI’s sharp 2026 pretraining progress to long-term research and computing investments, with automation playing a smaller part.
AHM calls OpenAI’s release of over 700 mathematical files a demonstration of power rather than scholarship.
The decimal points may be tidy; the comparisons aren’t.
A shared development limit needs measurements that different labs can meaningfully compare.
OpenAI calls the result the first autonomous AI solution to a prominent open problem in mathematics.
Pachocki hopes an initial limit, with explicit conditions for crossing it, would lead to a framework for setting successive ones.

passages: The post referred to Li as Century Longteng's chief strategy officer.ALSO READ | As Alice Huang pursued Nvidia chips, her husband built a $9 billion China data-center empireAt the time, the Biden administration had just curbed sales of Nvidia's semiconductors to China.

Chinese national Li Ming, who's currently out on bail in Singapore, was a central operator of a network of companies that smuggled restricted Nvidia AI chips into China, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter.Among these companies was Megaspeed, where Alice Huang was a managing director.

Meanwhile, he also played a key role in other companies trading Nvidia chips.The surfacing of new, previously unknown connections, such as Li Ming's, shows that the efforts to help China close the gap in the AI race went far beyond the Megaspeed row.In February 2025, Li, along with others, was charged with fraud in Singapore in connection with an alleged transhipment of Nvidia chips, according to the report.

In May 2025, records were requested from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed, and subsequently, in June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its internal "no-sell" list.ALSO READ | Nvidia ‘no longer’ shipping Hopper data centre AI chips to China as US tightens export curbsMeanwhile, in February 2025, Singapore also launched a probe into Megaspeed and several of its senior executives over suspected false declarations involving server purchases.

They acquired a Chinese video game company's Singapore unit and renamed it Megaspeed, with Alice Huang listed as a company director.Then, Megaspeed told Nvidia that Chinese tech giant Alibaba was an anchor customer and went on to become a member of the chipmaker's cloud partner programme in November 2023.

However, Alice Huang was given a stern warning and was barred from re-entering the country.Alice's husband, Kang Wei, was detained in Shanghai earlier this year as part of a probe into suspected stock-market manipulation, the WSJ reported.Notably, Megaspeed clarified allegations of chip smuggling and said that Alice Huang left the firm in August 2025.

Alice and her husband then set up a cloud-computing joint venture, Century Longteng, in 2021, according to Chinese corporate registry records cited by the report.Two years later, in January 2023, Li appeared in a photo on social media showing him visiting a Shanghai AI equipment company.

He will appear before a joint meeting of the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China Select committees on December 1, Bloomberg reported, citing a statement from the panels' chairman.Jensen Huang reportedly accepted the congressional invitation under the threat of a possible subpoena from Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast and China panel chair John Moolenaar to compel him to show up.

The entire row related to her and the affair with Jensen Huang led to his exit from Nvidia, triggering multiple investigations into the company's chip deals, Megaspeed and other related links.In this entire suspected spy-and-chip-smuggling scene, a new face has entered.
However, Chinese tech companies' sudden demand for the world's best AI chips had two possible reasons.
One, to legally access Nvidia computing abroad—a logistically difficult move that requires transferring large amounts of data across borders.

extraction.body: Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, has been at the centre of an alleged Chinese spy and suspected chip smuggling row ever since ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair. However, a 52-year-old Chinese national has now reportedly emerged as a key behind-the-scenes player.The United States suspected Alice Huang of being a Chinese spy, a claim that has been dismissed by Beijing. The entire row related to her and the affair with Jensen Huang led to his exit from Nvidia, triggering multiple investigations into the company's chip deals, Megaspeed and other related links.In this entire suspected spy-and-chip-smuggling scene, a new face has entered. Chinese national Li Ming, who's currently out on bail in Singapore, was a central operator of a network of companies that smuggled restricted Nvidia AI chips into China, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter.Among these companies was Megaspeed, where Alice Huang was a managing director. Li was reportedly involved neck-deep in Megaspeed's activities and was also a part of their major decisions. Meanwhile, he also played a key role in other companies trading Nvidia chips.The surfacing of new, previously unknown connections, such as Li Ming's, shows that the efforts to help China close the gap in the AI race went far beyond the Megaspeed row.In February 2025, Li, along with others, was charged with fraud in Singapore in connection with an alleged transhipment of Nvidia chips, according to the report. Several other companies had been named in the case, but not Megaspeed.How Li Ming routed Nvidia chips to ChinaLi allegedly purchased computer servers equipped with Nvidia chips on the pretext that the hardware was for his local firm, Luxuriate Your Life. Instead, he shipped those servers to Malaysia, from where they were later moved to an unknown third location.By the time charges were filed in Singapore, Li had been working with Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, for years, the WSJ report said. Alice and her husband then set up a cloud-computing joint venture, Century Longteng, in 2021, according to Chinese corporate registry records cited by the report.Two years later, in January 2023, Li appeared in a photo on social media showing him visiting a Shanghai AI equipment company. The post referred to Li as Century Longteng's chief strategy officer.ALSO READ | As Alice Huang pursued Nvidia chips, her husband built a $9 billion China data-center empireAt the time, the Biden administration had just curbed sales of Nvidia's semiconductors to China. However, Chinese tech companies' sudden demand for the world's best AI chips had two possible reasons. One, to legally access Nvidia computing abroad—a logistically difficult move that requires transferring large amounts of data across borders. Second, to smuggle hardware into China.Li, along with Alice Huang and Kang Wei, began setting up partners in Southeast Asia to bring advanced computing power to Chinese consumers, people familiar with the business said, according to the WSJ. They acquired a Chinese video game company's Singapore unit and renamed it Megaspeed, with Alice Huang listed as a company director.Then, Megaspeed told Nvidia that Chinese tech giant Alibaba was an anchor customer and went on to become a member of the chipmaker's cloud partner programme in November 2023. This played in Megaspeed's favour as the partner status allowed the company priority access to buy the latest chips.Megaspeed reportedly brought servers to Malaysia and provided offshore computing power to Alibaba. Some of these servers were also reportedly sent to a tech company called Century Litong in Shanghai in violation of the US export controls. An investigation into Megaspeed for potential export control violations was launched in 2024. In May 2025, records were requested from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed, and subsequently, in June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its internal "no-sell" list.ALSO READ | Nvidia ‘no longer’ shipping Hopper data centre AI chips to China as US tightens export curbsMeanwhile, in February 2025, Singapore also launched a probe into Megaspeed and several of its senior executives over suspected false declarations involving server purchases. In this investigation, insufficient evidence of criminal offences was found in Singapore. However, Alice Huang was given a stern warning and was barred from re-entering the country.Alice's husband, Kang Wei, was detained in Shanghai earlier this year as part of a probe into suspected stock-market manipulation, the WSJ reported.Notably, Megaspeed clarified allegations of chip smuggling and said that Alice Huang left the firm in August 2025. It also affirmed that it conducts "legitimate and lawful business."Jensen Huang's Nvidia exitJensen Huang's affairs with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, and an internal company employee, among others, cost him his 33-year-long stint at Nvidia.On November 12, Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive officer. The company's board said that he stepped down as president, CEO and board member with immediate effect.Nvidia's board of directors then appointed Colette Kress, its executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO. She will continue to serve in her previous roles alongside her interim office until a permanent replacement is appointed.ALSO READ | Indian-American executive Jay Puri oversaw Nvidia chip sales to Alice Huang: ReportThe chipmaker's board also launched an internal inquiry into Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, though it has already said that it doesn't believe national security or company secrets were compromised.In view of the ongoing row, Jensen Huang also reportedly agreed to brief the US Congress next month on his affair with a suspected Chinese spy. He will appear before a joint meeting of the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China Select committees on December 1, Bloomberg reported, citing a statement from the panels' chairman.Jensen Huang reportedly accepted the congressional invitation under the threat of a possible subpoena from Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast and China panel chair John Moolenaar to compel him to show up.

However, a 52-year-old Chinese national has now reportedly emerged as a key behind-the-scenes player. The United States suspected Alice Huang of being a Chinese spy, a claim dismissed by Beijing. The controversy surrounding her alleged affair with Jensen Huang led to his exit from Nvidia, triggering multiple investigations into the company's chip deals, Megaspeed and other related connections. A new figure has now emerged in the alleged spy and chip-smuggling controversy. Chinese national Li Ming, who is currently out on bail in Singapore, was a central operator of a network of companies that smuggled restricted Nvidia AI chips into China, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Among these companies was Megaspeed, where Alice Huang served as a managing director. Li was reportedly deeply involved in Megaspeed's activities and participated in major decisions. He also played a key role in other companies trading Nvidia chips. The emergence of previously unknown connections, such as Li Ming's, shows that efforts to help China close the gap in the AI race extended far beyond the Megaspeed controversy. In February 2025, Li, along with others, was charged with fraud in Singapore in connection with an alleged transhipment of Nvidia chips, according to the report. Several other companies were named in the case, but not Megaspeed. Li allegedly purchased computer servers equipped with Nvidia chips, claiming that the hardware was intended for his local firm, Luxuriate Your Life. However, prosecutors in Singapore alleged that this was a false claim. Instead, he shipped the servers to Malaysia, from where they were later moved to an unknown third location. By the time charges were filed in Singapore, Li had been working with Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, for years, the WSJ report said. Alice and her husband then established a cloud-computing joint venture, Century Longteng, in 2021, according to Chinese corporate registry records cited by the report. Two years later, in January 2023, Li appeared in a photograph shared on social media showing him visiting a Shanghai-based AI equipment company. The post identified Li as Century Longteng's chief strategy officer. At the time, the Biden administration had just restricted sales of Nvidia's semiconductors to China. However, Chinese technology companies' sudden demand for the world's leading AI chips had two possible explanations. One was to legally access Nvidia computing resources abroad, a logistically difficult process requiring large amounts of data to be transferred across borders. The second was to smuggle the hardware into China. Li, Alice Huang and Kang Wei began establishing partnerships in Southeast Asia to bring advanced computing power to Chinese consumers, people familiar with the business said, according to the WSJ. They acquired the Singapore unit of a Chinese video game company and renamed it Megaspeed, with Alice Huang listed as a company director. Megaspeed then told Nvidia that Chinese technology giant Alibaba was an anchor customer and became a member of the chipmaker's cloud partner programme in November 2023. This worked in Megaspeed's favour, as the partnership status gave the company priority access to purchase the latest chips. Megaspeed reportedly brought servers to Malaysia and provided offshore computing power to Alibaba. Some of these servers were also reportedly sent to a Shanghai-based technology company called Century Litong in violation of US export controls. Alice Huang and Kang Wei's Century Longteng was a major shareholder of Century Litong until 2024, the WSJ report said. While Alice Huang was reportedly having an extramarital affair with Jensen Huang to secure access to Nvidia's advanced computing chips, Kang was busy building a vast network of government-backed data centres across China, the WSJ had previously reported, citing a review of Chinese public records. From 2021 to 2024, proposed investments linked to Kang's network totalled more than $9 billion, all backed by the government. Although Alice Huang's pitch to Nvidia identifying Alibaba as a Megaspeed customer secured the company priority access to the chipmaker's products, her efforts were derailed in 2025 by Nvidia's internal investigation.
