In May 2025, records were requested from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. Subsequently, in June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its internal "no-sell" list. Meanwhile, Singapore launched a probe into Megaspeed and several of its senior executives in February 2025 over suspected false declarations involving server purchases. The investigation found insufficient evidence of criminal offences in Singapore. However, Alice Huang was given a stern warning and barred from re-entering the country. Alice's husband, Kang Wei, was detained in Shanghai earlier this year as part of an investigation into suspected stock market manipulation, the WSJ reported. Megaspeed has denied allegations of chip smuggling and said Alice Huang left the firm in August 2025. It also maintained that it conducts "legitimate and lawful business". Jensen Huang's alleged affairs with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy, and an internal company employee, among others, cost him his 33-year-long stint at Nvidia. On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive officer. The company's board said he stepped down as president, CEO and board member with immediate effect. Nvidia's board of directors then appointed Colette Kress, its executive vice-president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO. She will continue in her previous roles alongside her interim position until a permanent replacement is appointed. The chipmaker's board also launched an internal inquiry into Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, although it has already said it does not believe national security or company secrets were compromised. He will appear before a joint meeting of the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China Select committees on 1 December, Bloomberg reported, citing a statement from the panels' chairman. One was to legally access Nvidia computing resources abroad, a logistically difficult process requiring large amounts of data to be transferred across borders. The second was to smuggle the hardware into China. The United States suspected Alice Huang of being a Chinese spy, a claim dismissed by Beijing. The controversy surrounding her alleged affair with Jensen Huang led to his exit from Nvidia, triggering multiple investigations into the company's chip deals, Megaspeed and other related connections.

A new figure has now emerged in the alleged spy and chip-smuggling controversy. Chinese national Li Ming, who is currently out on bail in Singapore, was a central operator of a network of companies that smuggled restricted Nvidia AI chips into China, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

Among these companies was Megaspeed, where Alice Huang served as a managing director. Li was reportedly deeply involved in Megaspeed's activities and participated in major decisions. He also played a key role in other companies trading Nvidia chips.
The emergence of previously unknown connections, such as Li Ming's, shows that efforts to help China close the gap in the AI race extended far beyond the Megaspeed controversy.

In February 2025, Li, along with others, was charged with fraud in Singapore in connection with an alleged transhipment of Nvidia chips, according to the report. Several other companies were named in the case, but not Megaspeed.

Li allegedly purchased computer servers equipped with Nvidia chips, claiming that the hardware was intended for his local firm, Luxuriate Your Life. However, prosecutors in Singapore alleged that this was a false claim. Instead, he shipped the servers to Malaysia, from where they were later moved to an unknown third location.

By the time charges were filed in Singapore, Li had been working with Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, for years, the WSJ report said. Alice and her husband then established a cloud-computing joint venture, Century Longteng, in 2021, according to Chinese corporate registry records cited by the report.

One was to legally access Nvidia computing resources abroad, a logistically difficult process requiring large amounts of data to be transferred across borders. The second was to smuggle the hardware into China.

They acquired the Singapore unit of a Chinese video game company and renamed it Megaspeed, with Alice Huang listed as a company director.

Some of these servers were also reportedly sent to a Shanghai-based technology company called Century Litong in violation of US export controls. Alice Huang and Kang Wei's Century Longteng was a major shareholder of Century Litong until 2024, the WSJ report said.

While Alice Huang was reportedly having an extramarital affair with Jensen Huang to secure access to Nvidia's advanced computing chips, Kang was busy building a vast network of government-backed data centres across China, the WSJ had previously reported, citing a review of Chinese public records.
From 2021 to 2024, proposed investments linked to Kang's network totalled more than $9 billion, all backed by the government.

Although Alice Huang's pitch to Nvidia identifying Alibaba as a Megaspeed customer secured the company priority access to the chipmaker's products, her efforts were derailed in 2025 by Nvidia's internal investigation.
The US Departments of Commerce and Justice recently revealed details of their investigation into Megaspeed. A probe into potential export control violations by the company was launched in 2024.
In May 2025, records were requested from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. Subsequently, in June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its internal "no-sell" list.

Meanwhile, Singapore launched a probe into Megaspeed and several of its senior executives in February 2025 over suspected false declarations involving server purchases. The investigation found insufficient evidence of criminal offences in Singapore. However, Alice Huang was given a stern warning and barred from re-entering the country.
Alice's husband, Kang Wei, was detained in Shanghai earlier this year as part of an investigation into suspected stock market manipulation, the WSJ reported.
Megaspeed has denied allegations of chip smuggling and said Alice Huang left the firm in August 2025. It also maintained that it conducts "legitimate and lawful business".

In light of the ongoing controversy, Jensen Huang also reportedly agreed to brief the US Congress next month about his affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
He will appear before a joint meeting of the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China Select committees on 1 December, Bloomberg reported, citing a statement from the panels' chairman.

Jensen Huang reportedly accepted the congressional invitation under the threat of a possible subpoena from Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast and China Select Committee Chairman John Moolenaar to compel him to appear.

WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump on Friday said the US wants only older chips to be sold to China, adding that his administration was discussing an agreement with China, without providing further details.

"We want only older chips, and we don't mind if none go. But only older. You have to understand, China makes chips too, and if we're not going to sell them, they'll make them themselves," he told reporters at a press conference following his trip to Asia.

Those remarks followed an earlier answer to a question about whether he was considering easing up export bans on chips to China after meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, to which Trump responded: "We're talking about a very comprehensive deal with China."
Trump's administration on Monday, ahead of the trip, said it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips from companies like Nvidia.

passages: The intelligence chief said the upgrades were necessary to improve system performance and strengthen cybersecurity as rapid technological advances put increasing pressure on older infrastructure.A series of technology failures this month disrupted several critical US systems.

Americans should expect more technology outages and service disruptions as companies and government agencies upgrade ageing systems, US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Sunday, warning that glitches are inevitable during the transition."During that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service.

These included a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage affecting email services, a technical glitch impacting several major banks and a temporary disruption to the National Security Agency's network.Speaking on ABC's *This Week*, Clayton reiterated that the outages were not caused by coordinated or state-sponsored attacks, maintaining that they were linked to technical upgrades.However, he declined to comment on separate reports of cyberattacks targeting the FBI and the Department of Agriculture.

extraction.body: US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has warned that further technology outages may strike the country as private corporations and government agencies modernise infrastructure and fortify cybersecurity defences. Speaking on CNN's "State of the Union" , Clayton cautioned that the public should prepare for temporary service interruptions whilst institutions invest heavily in upgrading digital systems to adapt to advancements in artificial intelligence (AI). "The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road," Clayton said. He noted that organisations are actively addressing the transitions to limit long-term fallout. The caution follows a series of high-profile technical failures that disrupted commercial flights, digital enterprise services, and retail banking transactions across the country, involving the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Microsoft Outlook, and JPMorgan Chase. Federal officials have largely dismissed speculation linking the incidents to a coordinated foreign cyberattack or AI-driven sabotage, stating that independent assessments point to distinct, isolated technical faults. The warning coincided with fresh travel chaos on Sunday as Delta Air Lines encountered nationwide flight delays stemming from an operational breakdown at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, its primary hub. passages: US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has warned that further technology outages may strike the country as private corporations and government agencies modernise infrastructure and fortify cybersecurity defences.

Speaking on CNN's "State of the Union" , Clayton cautioned that the public should prepare for temporary service interruptions whilst institutions invest heavily in upgrading digital systems to adapt to advancements in artificial intelligence (AI).

"The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road," Clayton said.
He noted that organisations are actively addressing the transitions to limit long-term fallout.

The caution follows a series of high-profile technical failures that disrupted commercial flights, digital enterprise services, and retail banking transactions across the country, involving the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Microsoft Outlook, and JPMorgan Chase.

Federal officials have largely dismissed speculation linking the incidents to a coordinated foreign cyberattack or AI-driven sabotage, stating that independent assessments point to distinct, isolated technical faults.

The warning coincided with fresh travel chaos on Sunday as Delta Air Lines encountered nationwide flight delays stemming from an operational breakdown at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, its primary hub.
Delta attributed the operational disruption to a software malfunction in its automated system used to calculate aircraft weight and balance before take-off.
"Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation," the carrier confirmed in an official statement.

Nvidia's financial performance and outlook should come as a relief for investors during a difficult time. The company's co-founder Jensen Huang recently resigned as CEO, and Nvidia is now in the hunt for a new one. However, comments from interim CEO Colette Kress on the latest earnings call clearly suggest that the company's growth prospects remain solid. Nvidia's revenue increased by 103% year-over-year last quarter to $115.8 billion, driven by a 110% jump in data center revenue. The company anticipates $130 billion in revenue for the current quarter, an improvement of 91% over the year-ago quarter. Even better, Nvidia has raised its fiscal 2028 revenue guidance to 75%, up from the prior expectation of 70%. So, I won't be surprised to see this artificial intelligence (AI) specialist go on a bull run once again. But if you're still on the sidelines about Nvidia's prospects, it may be a good idea to take a closer look at another semiconductor stock -- ASML Holding ( ASML -6.63% ) . Here's why. Nvidia's impressive data center growth in the previous quarter was driven by the incredible demand for its latest-generation Vera Rubin chip systems. The company noted that the Vera Rubin platform generated almost $20 billion in revenue last quarter, "making it the fastest product ramp in Nvidia's history." The company noted that Rubin deployments will continue improving in 2027. Moreover, Nvidia management remarked that demand for its chips is outpacing supply. All this bodes well for ASML Holding, which manufactures the advanced chipmaking equipment that enables Nvidia to make the advanced Blackwell and Vera Rubin processors. Nvidia's Vera Rubin chip is built on a 3-nanometer (nm) process node, while the previous-generation Blackwell architecture, which remains in solid demand, is built on a 4-nm process node. These small process nodes are manufactured using extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines, and ASML holds a near monopoly in this market. Not surprisingly, ASML has seen a significant increase in demand for its lithography machines. The company sold 113 new lithography systems in the third quarter of 2026, up from 66 in the year-ago period. As demand for advanced AI chips exceeds supply, ASML is looking to increase the production capacity of its EUV lithography machines. The company aims to increase the production of machines that make advanced chips by 30% in 2027. What's more, it is exploring the possibility of enhancing capacity by more than 30% in 2028. ASML's customer base includes Nvidia's foundry partner, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing , Samsung , Intel , and Micron Technology , among others. This diversified customer base means that ASML stands to gain from both the foundry/logic and memory markets, making it a safer bet than Nvidia. Additionally, ASML is now growing at a nice clip, driven by the increasing demand for its EUV machines. AP-Yonhap WASHINGTON — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday he was frustrated with the Commerce Department’s delay in implementing restrictions over the export of certain Nvidia chips to China. Bessent said on CNBC that his department, along with the departments of State and Defense and the U.S. Trade Representative, were in favor of adding Megaspeed to an export control list for months but that the Commerce Department was in charge of the matter. “I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s,” he said, referring to an older generation of the company's advanced AI chips. Commerce “has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes.” Bessent's comments were an unusually public rebuke of the Commerce Department, which oversees U.S. government controls over exports of sensitive, high-tech goods. The comments come as Nvidia’s ties to Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which prominently touts the companies’ partnership on its website, play a prominent role in the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Huang allegedly had an affair with the CEO of Megaspeed, Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence suspects is a Chinese spy, the New York Times has reported. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has come under increasing scrutiny because of his reportedly close relationship with Huang. The Times reported Thursday that Lutnick resisted placing greater limits on the sale of Nvidia's more advanced chips to China. Chinese firms have accessed Nvidia's chips through companies like Megaspeed, which has purchased more than $4 billion worth of Nvidia's advanced semiconductors. The split in President Donald Trump's cabinet reflects the widespread fallout from the scandal that has engulfed Nvidia, one of the most valuable publicly-traded companies in the world. Nvidia's computer chips play a central role in the buildout of artificial intelligence, powering AI models such as those developed by Open AI and Anthropic. The U.S. government has, since the Biden administration, sought to restrict the sale of the most advanced AI computer chips to China in an effort to protect U.S. technology companies' lead. Yet China has at times retaliated, creating controversy over how far the U.S. should push its restrictions. The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment. Bessent declined to comment Friday on the Times report that he confronted Lutnick last week in the White House's situation room. Separately, Axios reported this week that Lutnick received a classified memo this spring warning about Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected spy. Numerous members of Congress have said they will investigate Lutnick's actions and called for him to testify on Capitol Hill. Richard Neal, both Democrats, wrote Lutnick a letter demanding that he preserve all records related to decisions about Nvidia chip exports, pending an investigation. Trump's approval of advanced Nvidia chip exports to China “raises critical questions about whether and to what extent political considerations are improperly influencing policy decisions made by the Administration,” Wyden and Neal wrote. John Kennedy of Louisiana, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, said he has questions for the commerce secretary and urged him to hold a press conference to explain what he knew. “The Commerce Department greenlit $4 billion of sales of advanced chips to the company of the spy that Mr. Huang was having an affair with and I want to know why," Kennedy said. "I want to know why the Commerce Department did it in light of the export controls, and everything I read indicates that this was a decision by the secretary himself." Kennedy added that Lutnick should testify before the Senate and should be subpoenaed if necessary. Huang resigned Thursday after news that he had an affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence suspects to be a Chinese spy, according to The Times. AP-Yonhap WASHINGTON — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday he was frustrated with the Commerce Department’s delay in implementing restrictions over the export of certain Nvidia chips to China. Bessent said on CNBC that his department, along with the departments of State and Defense and the U.S. Trade Representative, were in favor of adding Megaspeed to an export control list for months but that the Commerce Department was in charge of the matter. “I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s,” he said, referring to an older generation of the company's advanced AI chips. Commerce “has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes.” Bessent's comments were an unusually public rebuke of the Commerce Department, which oversees U.S. government controls over exports of sensitive, high-tech goods. The comments come as Nvidia’s ties to Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which prominently touts the companies’ partnership on its website, play a prominent role in the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Huang allegedly had an affair with the CEO of Megaspeed, Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence suspects is a Chinese spy, the New York Times has reported. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has come under increasing scrutiny because of his reportedly close relationship with Huang. The Times reported Thursday that Lutnick resisted placing greater limits on the sale of Nvidia's more advanced chips to China. Chinese firms have accessed Nvidia's chips through companies like Megaspeed, which has purchased more than $4 billion worth of Nvidia's advanced semiconductors. The split in President Donald Trump's cabinet reflects the widespread fallout from the scandal that has engulfed Nvidia, one of the most valuable publicly-traded companies in the world. Nvidia's computer chips play a central role in the buildout of artificial intelligence, powering AI models such as those developed by Open AI and Anthropic. The U.S. government has, since the Biden administration, sought to restrict the sale of the most advanced AI computer chips to China in an effort to protect U.S. technology companies' lead. Yet China has at times retaliated, creating controversy over how far the U.S. should push its restrictions. The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment. Bessent declined to comment Friday on the Times report that he confronted Lutnick last week in the White House's situation room. Separately, Axios reported this week that Lutnick received a classified memo this spring warning about Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected spy. Numerous members of Congress have said they will investigate Lutnick's actions and called for him to testify on Capitol Hill. Richard Neal, both Democrats, wrote Lutnick a letter demanding that he preserve all records related to decisions about Nvidia chip exports, pending an investigation. Trump's approval of advanced Nvidia chip exports to China “raises critical questions about whether and to what extent political considerations are improperly influencing policy decisions made by the Administration,” Wyden and Neal wrote. John Kennedy of Louisiana, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, said he has questions for the commerce secretary and urged him to hold a press conference to explain what he knew. “The Commerce Department greenlit $4 billion of sales of advanced chips to the company of the spy that Mr. Huang was having an affair with and I want to know why," Kennedy said. "I want to know why the Commerce Department did it in light of the export controls, and everything I read indicates that this was a decision by the secretary himself." Kennedy added that Lutnick should testify before the Senate and should be subpoenaed if necessary. Huang resigned Thursday after news that he had an affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence suspects to be a Chinese spy, according to The Times. Last year, Megaspeed was accused of illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was “no evidence” of such exports. On Thursday, Megaspeed maintained it takes its obligation to comply with American export control laws “extremely seriously” — and that it was committed to working “constructively and transparently” with the U.S. government.

Trump's approval of advanced Nvidia chip exports to China “raises critical questions about whether and to what extent political considerations are improperly influencing policy decisions made by the Administration,” Wyden and Neal wrote.
Last year, Megaspeed was accused of illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was “no evidence” of such exports.
Bessent declined to comment Friday on the Times report that he confronted Lutnick last week in the White House's situation room.
Chinese firms have accessed Nvidia's chips through companies like Megaspeed, which has purchased more than $4 billion worth of Nvidia's advanced semiconductors.
Nvidia's computer chips play a central role in the buildout of artificial intelligence, powering AI models such as those developed by Open AI and Anthropic.
Numerous members of Congress have said they will investigate Lutnick's actions and called for him to testify on Capitol Hill.
The split in President Donald Trump's cabinet reflects the widespread fallout from the scandal that has engulfed Nvidia, one of the most valuable publicly-traded companies in the world.
Separately, Axios reported this week that Lutnick received a classified memo this spring warning about Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected spy.

The dispute centers on Megaspeed International, which the Guardian says facilitated about $12 billion in chip sales that violated U.S. export controls, and allegations that Commerce delayed action despite warnings.
Separately, Bessent says officials are asking Nvidia who was responsible for compliance, putting both federal enforcement decisions and corporate controls under scrutiny.
Kennedy said he was less interested in former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang ’s reported personal conduct than in how U.S. restrictions were apparently bypassed.
He said the administration had contacted the company’s temporary management, lead directors and lawyers as it tried to identify who held that responsibility.
Other administration officials, including Bessent, wanted Megaspeed placed on a trade blacklist, but the Commerce Department stalled enforcement.
That dispute places the department’s decisions—not only Nvidia’s sales practices—under scrutiny.
The administration has prohibited sales of advanced AI chips to China.

Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO on November 12 after allegations surfaced of extramarital relationships with Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees, the Guardian reported.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was an executive director of Megaspeed.
The newspaper describes her as a suspected Chinese spy; that remains an allegation.

extraction.body: Bessent also withheld support for Jensen Huang's return as CEO, saying investigations should conclude before a leader is chosen. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that Nvidia has yet to explain how its AI chips reached China, and he withheld support for Jensen Huang's return as CEO. The United States is investigating whether Nvidia gave China access to advanced AI chips despite government restrictions, CBS News reported. On Nov. 15, Bessent gave Nvidia 10 days to answer questions about its compliance with export rules in an interview with Fox News. Seven days into that period, Bessent appeared on CBS's "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" and said the administration still lacked the answers it sought. "We don't, Margaret," he said. Officials have contacted Nvidia's interim management, lead directors and lawyers, Bessent said. "It behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was," he said. "We do need to see who was in charge of compliance there," Bessent said. He also asked, "Was it at the lower levels? Was it at the middle levels? Did it go all the way to the top?". During his Nov. 15 Fox News interview, Bessent raised the possibility of a "culture of noncompliance" at Nvidia and asked whether it was "pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings." He said Sunday that such a culture was only a possibility. "We will see, and that's why I think the board is moving very quickly to establish whether this did or did not exist," he said. Asked about Nvidia's reported "handshake" business approach, Bessent said, "For deals that size, there's no such thing as an untraceable handshake deal." The shipments of chips left financial and documentary trails, he said. "They may not be the 100-page documents, but it will be possible to understand what has gone on here," he said. Bessent said he had confidence that Nvidia's internal committees "will come up with some very fulsome and robust answers." Bessent said the investigations should conclude before Nvidia's next leader is decided. Asked about Huang's return, he said, "I think we have to see where the buck stops," and asked, "Were these malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the noncompliance?". President Donald Trump took a different position at a news conference Friday, saying he wanted Huang to return as chief executive. "I think the company, if they were smart, they'd take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work," Trump said earlier. Huang resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, one involving Alice Huang, an alleged spy according to CBS News. The New York Times reported that Huang stepped down after acknowledging an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence had identified as a Chinese asset. Bessent called the affair "kind of a canard" and said company culture mattered more than one person's foibles. "I assume that he didn't know that she was an alleged spy," he said. The Justice and Commerce Departments said last week that they were pursuing a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore company Alice Huang once led. Officials are examining whether Megaspeed smuggled Nvidia chips into China, while the Securities and Exchange Commission, or SEC, is investigating Nvidia's accounting practices, according to the Times. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has led Nvidia since Huang's departure. Bessent said last week that he thought Nvidia's leadership needed a major shake-up. He has urged the company to appoint an outsider to run it. It was not immediately known whether Nvidia will deliver the answers before Bessent's 10-day window closes. Huang is scheduled to testify at a private House hearing on Dec. 1; he is also expected to appear before the Senate Banking Committee.

extraction.body: Bessent also withheld support for Jensen Huang's return as CEO, saying investigations should conclude before a leader is chosen. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that Nvidia has yet to explain how its AI chips reached China, and he withheld support for Jensen Huang's return as CEO. The United States is investigating whether Nvidia gave China access to advanced AI chips despite government restrictions, CBS News reported. On Nov. 15, Bessent gave Nvidia 10 days to answer questions about its compliance with export rules in an interview with Fox News. Seven days into that period, Bessent appeared on CBS's "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" and said the administration still lacked the answers it sought. "We don't, Margaret," he said. Officials have contacted Nvidia's interim management, lead directors and lawyers, Bessent said. "It behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was," he said. "We do need to see who was in charge of compliance there," Bessent said. He also asked, "Was it at the lower levels? Was it at the middle levels? Did it go all the way to the top?". During his Nov. 15 Fox News interview, Bessent raised the possibility of a "culture of noncompliance" at Nvidia and asked whether it was "pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings." He said Sunday that such a culture was only a possibility. "We will see, and that's why I think the board is moving very quickly to establish whether this did or did not exist," he said. Asked about Nvidia's reported "handshake" business approach, Bessent said, "For deals that size, there's no such thing as an untraceable handshake deal." The shipments of chips left financial and documentary trails, he said. "They may not be the 100-page documents, but it will be possible to understand what has gone on here," he said. Bessent said he had confidence that Nvidia's internal committees "will come up with some very fulsome and robust answers." Bessent said the investigations should conclude before Nvidia's next leader is decided. Asked about Huang's return, he said, "I think we have to see where the buck stops," and asked, "Were these malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the noncompliance?". President Donald Trump took a different position at a news conference Friday, saying he wanted Huang to return as chief executive. "I think the company, if they were smart, they'd take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work," Trump said earlier. Huang resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, one involving Alice Huang, an alleged spy according to CBS News. The New York Times reported that Huang stepped down after acknowledging an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence had identified as a Chinese asset. Bessent called the affair "kind of a canard" and said company culture mattered more than one person's foibles. "I assume that he didn't know that she was an alleged spy," he said. The Justice and Commerce Departments said last week that they were pursuing a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore company Alice Huang once led. Officials are examining whether Megaspeed smuggled Nvidia chips into China, while the Securities and Exchange Commission, or SEC, is investigating Nvidia's accounting practices, according to the Times. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has led Nvidia since Huang's departure. Bessent said last week that he thought Nvidia's leadership needed a major shake-up. He has urged the company to appoint an outsider to run it. It was not immediately known whether Nvidia will deliver the answers before Bessent's 10-day window closes. Huang is scheduled to testify at a private House hearing on Dec. 1; he is also expected to appear before the Senate Banking Committee.

sources.title: Bessent says we "need answers" on role Nvidia played in sending AI chips to China, suggests Alice Huang is "kind of a canard"
passages: Washington — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that the administration needs answers from Nvidia as questions swirl about whether it has complied with export restrictions, after revelations surrounding its CEO's alleged affairs sent the chipmaker into crisis."We do need answers," Bessent said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."After Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO amid revelations about extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged spy, the U.S. is investigating how Nvidia may have given China access to advanced AI computer chips, despite government restrictions.

When pressed on whether he thinks it would be a good idea for Jensen Huang to return, Bessent said, "I think we have to see where the buck stops — Were these malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the noncompliance?" He also drew a distinction between this possible dynamic, and Jensen Huang's alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang."I think that is kind of a canard," Bessent said.

"They may not be the 100-page documents, but it will be possible to understand what has gone on here."On his call for an inquiry into whether Nvidia had a culture of noncompliance, Bessent said that it's simply a possibility that the dynamic was at play."We will see, and that's why I think the board is moving very quickly to establish whether this did or did not exist," Bessent said.
"It behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was." Nvidia's CFO, Colette Kress, has taken the helm after Huang's departure.
"We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers," Bessent said.

Last week, Bessent referenced a possible "culture of noncompliance" at Nvidia, questioning whether the company was "pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings." In an interview on Fox News, Bessent said he needed answers from Nvidia on its compliance with export restrictions within 10 days. But Bessent has urged the company to bring someone in from the outside to run the company. Asked whether the president understands the risks that Bessent has pointed to, Bessent replied that it remained to be seen "which level of the business knew about this.""Was it at the lower levels? And I have confidence that the Nvidia committees are moving very quickly on this and will come up with some very fulsome and robust answers," he said. "Was there a culture of compliance versus one person's foibles?"Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee and will also be interviewed by House panels in early December.

extraction.body: Volunteers in black uniforms and body armour increasingly seen with figures such as Tommy Robinson There is a worrying rise in “reckless and intimidating” vigilantes posing as security guards around far-right figures, security experts have said. In recent months, uniformed figures wearing all black and body armour have been seen in the entourages of far-right figures including the convicted criminal Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, who goes by the name Tommy Robinson , and Paul Golding, the leader of the far-right political party Britain First. This group of “security volunteers” has also been seen at far-right protests, most recently this week in London and in Oxford, where the controversial “race philosopher” Nathan Cofnas was due to speak. They were seen scuffling with anti-racism protesters. They have also provided security for the rightwing provocateur Katie Hopkins. The ensemble calls itself British Security UK (BSUK), and says it is a volunteer-led security group. Those who join it are given all-black uniforms featuring black and white union flags, and they are not required to have any security qualifications or training. Usually security guards are asked to have a Security Industry Authority (SIA) qualification, meaning they know how to de-escalate situations, only use proportionate force and are trained in keeping members of the public safe. The website for the “security service” carries the disclaimer: “BSUK is not the police. Wearing BSUK uniform does not confer police powers. Any security services requiring an SIA licence must be carried out by appropriately licensed personnel. For emergencies, call 999.” The registered director of BSUK is Anthony Roberts, 53, who has volunteered as a security guard for Yaxley-Lennon and Golding. He wears combat trousers, a union jack-emblazoned body armour kit, and has facial tattoos. Posting on social media, he said “the police never handle the left properly … [they] let them run riot” because of “DEI training”. He said his organisation was “there to observe the police do their job, hold them accountable to the very laws we live under, and showcase the two-tier society we all live under”. He appears to share political views with those his group “protects”. sources.title: FBI investigating apparent hack of its key national criminal justice database, AP source says
passages: WASHINGTON — The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of a national law enforcement database that it maintains, a person familiar with the matter said Saturday.

The National Crime Information Center, known as the NCIC, is a computerized database of criminal justice information that is available to local, state and federal law enforcement agencies and includes records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history data, stolen property and other topics.

In September, for instance, a criminal hacking group known as ShinyHunters revealed that it had obtained a massive trove of data on FBI employees and applicants and had compromised the bureau’s jobs portal.

News that the NCIC was targeted comes as the country has encountered a series of digital outages in the government and private sector that Trump administration officials have said were caused by routine efforts to upgrade computer systems and fix vulnerabilities, rather than a cyberattack.
There was no immediate indication that the FBI incident was related to those outages.
Asked about the subject on Saturday, President Donald Trump said in a Fox News Channel interview: “We just heard about it, and I will say that it’s not good.”

In September, for instance, a criminal hacking group known as ShinyHunters revealed that it had obtained a massive trove of data on FBI employees and applicants and had compromised the bureau’s jobs portal. News that the NCIC was targeted comes as the country has encountered a series of digital outages in the government and private sector that Trump administration officials have said were caused by routine efforts to upgrade computer systems and fix vulnerabilities, rather than a cyberattack. There was no immediate indication that the FBI incident was related to those outages. Asked about the subject on Saturday, President Donald Trump said in a Fox News Channel interview: “We just heard about it, and I will say that it’s not good.”

extraction.body: A new era of disruptive cyber outages is making the nonstop data breaches of just a few years ago seem quaint. You don't have to subscribe to TikTok conspiracy theories to acknowledge that something feels different this time around. A host of mainstream technology failures has left Americans physically stranded, locked out of accounts, and unable to work. The recent cascade of breaks and digital dislocations feels like a preview to a more chaotic and disordered world, where everything is connected but also vulnerable and exploitable. AI is accelerating innovation, but it's also supercharging the capabilities of bad actors and increasing the blast radius for outages and overall online messiness. Even before the added messes on Monday (and Tuesday), Saturday Night Live lampooned the chaos with host John Mulaney listing the mess-ups in response to (fake) Peter Thiel asking, "Name one time that technology has let us down." Here's a brief rundown of what we've seen over the past week. For about 36 hours, much of corporate America's productivity suite went offline. Microsoft's signature platforms, including Outlook and Teams, stopped working . More than 70 countries and territories experienced the outage, hampering millions of users. "This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents," Microsoft explained. "The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change." National flight grounding and FAA ATC outage — Nov. 13 The Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop for more than four hours, unleashing a wave of delays and cancellations across the country. Outdated air traffic communications equipment and copper cable upgrades were to blame. While the stoppage lasted a handful of hours , its impacts rippled across air travel for several days as airlines scrambled to rebook passengers and get aircraft and crew back in place. The incident has become a political headache for the Trump administration and highlighted the nation's aging telecommunications infrastructure and its vulnerabilities. JPMorgan (and others) banking outage — Nov. 16 Thousands of customers reported problems with their online banking services at several major institutions, tied back to a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase. JPMorgan Chase said in a statement that it "has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems," adding that "there is no evidence this is cyber-related." The disruption, coming on the heels of the other major outages, sparked concerns that the events were connected, and that hackers were to blame. Users who made transactions involving Chase and other banks made it appear that the outage was systemic, but Chase said its banking platform was responsible. Just a few days after the massive national FAA groundstop, United Airlines had a stop of its own as yet another aviation-related technology failure occurred. Web-based apps that helped pilots fine-tune weight and balance on the aircraft were reportedly among the problems . The attack targeted Optimizely, an AI platform that lets companies design websites. Researchers at the cybersecurity firm Report URI identified the attack on Monday. In a post on its website Tuesday, Optimizely said that "an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability" in its Experimentation tool. "We've fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects," it said. As we were writing about this, CNN reported that the US National Security Communications network has gone down. Given that the NSA uses this network to communicate, it sounds like a big deal. On the other hand, President Trump says it's not,. "Things ​like that happen, it's fine," he told reporters in Manila . Neither CNN nor the NSA elaborated on the causes, but said there was currently no evidence of a cyberattack. A spokesperson for the NSA gave the following statement: "The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance. While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events." Charles Schwab users reported an outage on the brokerage app on Tuesday. More than 1,000 users reported a disruption, according to the website Downdetector . Schwab said in a statement, "A brief webpage loading issue has been resolved. Trading remained available, and clients could access their accounts at schwab.com/login or through the Schwab Mobile app. We apologize for the inconvenience." According to Downdetector, a large suite of Apple ( AAPL ) services including iCloud, Apple Card, Sign in with Apple and others were experiencing outages. Apple confirmed the outage but didn't add any details. As our rundown shows, there isn't one chief cause here despite the apparent acceleration in things breaking. But the web of causes is interconnected — just like our systems — and there is good reason to expect that things are getting worse with more cascades of breaks and digital dislocations. Everything is connected, and everything is more vulnerable and exploitable. The first and most obvious thing is cybersecurity. In the wake of the Binance hack — which was a major heist — founder Changpeng "CZ" Zhao told us that "banks are probably getting hacked left and right" as the cybersecurity landscape changes with AI-powered bad actors. The big question in the wake of that hack was how much AI was involved. With powerful AI tools, more "zero-day" bugs are likely to be found exploited, more social engineering can happen at scale, and even more tracks can be covered — leaving vulnerabilities open for longer. The rise of tools like Claude Code is another potential pitfall for these outages. Never before has it been easier to "vibecode," and companies looking to swap out engineers with Claude subscriptions may be deploying code that's not quite ready for primetime. This is, of course, speculation, as we haven't heard enough detail about any of these specific outages to point to this. What's not speculation, though, is that the sheer quantity of code output that's possible has meant the bottleneck is often now reviewing code — not writing it. And with extremely heavy output expectations on engineers, the code equivalent of a typo going through to publication is a new, modern risk. This story has been updated with new information on the Apple and NSA outages.

You don't have to subscribe to TikTok conspiracy theories to acknowledge that something feels different this time around. A host of mainstream technology failures has left Americans physically stranded, locked out of accounts, and unable to work.

The recent cascade of breaks and digital dislocations feels like a preview to a more chaotic and disordered world, where everything is connected but also vulnerable and exploitable. AI is accelerating innovation, but it's also supercharging the capabilities of bad actors and increasing the blast radius for outages and overall online messiness.

Even before the added messes on Monday (and Tuesday), Saturday Night Live lampooned the chaos with host John Mulaney listing the mess-ups in response to (fake) Peter Thiel asking, "Name one time that technology has let us down."
Here's a brief rundown of what we've seen over the past week.

For about 36 hours, much of corporate America's productivity suite went offline. Microsoft's signature platforms, including Outlook and Teams, stopped working . More than 70 countries and territories experienced the outage, hampering millions of users.

"This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents," Microsoft explained. "The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change."
National flight grounding and FAA ATC outage — Nov. 13

The Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop for more than four hours, unleashing a wave of delays and cancellations across the country. Outdated air traffic communications equipment and copper cable upgrades were to blame.

While the stoppage lasted a handful of hours , its impacts rippled across air travel for several days as airlines scrambled to rebook passengers and get aircraft and crew back in place. The incident has become a political headache for the Trump administration and highlighted the nation's aging telecommunications infrastructure and its vulnerabilities.
JPMorgan (and others) banking outage — Nov. 16
Thousands of customers reported problems with their online banking services at several major institutions, tied back to a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase.
JPMorgan Chase said in a statement that it "has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems," adding that "there is no evidence this is cyber-related."
The disruption, coming on the heels of the other major outages, sparked concerns that the events were connected, and that hackers were to blame.
Users who made transactions involving Chase and other banks made it appear that the outage was systemic, but Chase said its banking platform was responsible.

Given that the NSA uses this network to communicate, it sounds like a big deal. On the other hand, President Trump says it's not,.
"Things ​like that happen, it's fine," he told reporters in Manila .
Neither CNN nor the NSA elaborated on the causes, but said there was currently no evidence of a cyberattack.

A spokesperson for the NSA gave the following statement: "The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance. While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. Schwab said in a statement, "A brief webpage loading issue has been resolved. Trading remained available, and clients could access their accounts at schwab.com/login or through the Schwab Mobile app. We apologize for the inconvenience."

Currently, Bitcoin trades around $60,763, 51.8% below its all-time high of $126,080 set on October 6, 2025. In its latest 24-hour session, its price moved between $58,696 and $61,447.

Bitcoin’s decline has been long and significant. Market analyst Charlie Bilello pointed out on November 21, 2026, that Bitcoin had dropped 56% from its peak to its low, marking the longest peak-to-trough decline in its history and lasting 411 days.

Despite this downturn, the $1 million target continues to generate interest. Bernstein, a Wall Street research firm, has set a long-term target of about $1 million by 2033, and long-term holders often cite it as a potential destination for Bitcoin. So, can Bitcoin still reach $1 million by 2035?

Market capitalization is the total value of a cryptocurrency, calculated by multiplying its price by the number of coins in circulation. If Bitcoin reached $1 million per coin, its market value would soar to around $20.12 trillion, up from about $1.22 trillion now. This required gain of 1,546% translates to an annual increase of roughly 36% over the 9.1 years remaining until the end of 2035.

Bitcoin’s growing supply adds another layer of difficulty to this target. When Bitcoin closed at $8,118 on November 22, 2017, its entire market cap was about $135.5 billion. Now, with approximately 20.1 million coins in circulation out of a maximum of 21 million, every dollar increase in price adds significantly more value than it did in 2017.

Reaching a market cap of $20.12 trillion would put Bitcoin in the same league as gold, a comparison supporters often use. However, gold is currently trading around $3,536 per ounce, down 33% from $5,279 at the end of February 2026, suggesting this benchmark has also declined.

Bernstein bases its projections on Bitcoin’s four-year cycle, which is linked to the halving, an event that reduces the reward for mining new coins roughly every four years. Under Bernstein’s main scenario, Bitcoin could reach $150,000 by mid-2027, climb to about $300,000 in 2029, and near $1 million by 2033. However, this same report anticipated Bitcoin would rebound to $125,000 by late 2026, and Bitcoin is currently trading far below that level.

Spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) hold Bitcoin, so their purchases pull coins off the market. SoSoValue data indicates that cumulative net inflows to spot Bitcoin ETFs fell from $57.62 billion on October 29 to $53.51 billion on November 19.

On November 19 alone, these funds recorded $582 million in net outflows, and they took in money on only six trading days between October 23 and November 19. The total net assets of Bitcoin ETFs dropped to $76.55 billion from $104.88 billion on October 28, squeezed by both outflows and declining prices.

The Federal Reserve raised its upper limit to 4.00% from 3.75% in September, and markets are bracing for another possible rate hike on December 9. Kendrick has cautioned that if this tightening continues, Bitcoin could drop to about $50,000, 18% below its current price.

passages: For Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) to reach $1 million by 2035, it must gain about 1,546%. Over the past year, this goal has become even harder to reach. Currently, Bitcoin trades around $60,763, 51.8% below its all-time high of $126,080 set on October 6, 2025. In its latest 24-hour session, its price moved between $58,696 and $61,447.

Bitcoin’s decline has been long and significant. Market analyst Charlie Bilello pointed out on November 21, 2026, that Bitcoin had dropped 56% from its peak to its low, marking the longest peak-to-trough decline in its history and lasting 411 days.

Despite this downturn, the $1 million target continues to generate interest. Bernstein, a Wall Street research firm, has set a long-term target of about $1 million by 2033, and long-term holders often cite it as a potential destination for Bitcoin. So, can Bitcoin still reach $1 million by 2035?

Market capitalization is the total value of a cryptocurrency, calculated by multiplying its price by the number of coins in circulation. If Bitcoin reached $1 million per coin, its market value would soar to around $20.12 trillion, up from about $1.22 trillion now. This required gain of 1,546% translates to an annual increase of roughly 36% over the 9.1 years remaining until the end of 2035.

Bitcoin’s growing supply adds another layer of difficulty to this target. When Bitcoin closed at $8,118 on November 22, 2017, its entire market cap was about $135.5 billion. Now, with approximately 20.1 million coins in circulation out of a maximum of 21 million, every dollar increase in price adds significantly more value than it did in 2017.

Reaching a market cap of $20.12 trillion would put Bitcoin in the same league as gold, a comparison supporters often use. However, gold is currently trading around $3,536 per ounce, down 33% from $5,279 at the end of February 2026, suggesting this benchmark has also declined.

Bernstein bases its projections on Bitcoin’s four-year cycle, which is linked to the halving, an event that reduces the reward for mining new coins roughly every four years. Under Bernstein’s main scenario, Bitcoin could reach $150,000 by mid-2027, climb to about $300,000 in 2029, and near $1 million by 2033. However, this same report anticipated Bitcoin would rebound to $125,000 by late 2026, and Bitcoin is currently trading far below that level.

Standard Chartered has a more cautious outlook. The bank pushed its $500,000 target back from 2028 to 2030 in December 2025. In April 2026, analyst Geoffrey Kendrick set a year-end price target of $100,000. Even this $100,000 goal now seems ambitious.

Spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) hold Bitcoin, so their purchases pull coins off the market. SoSoValue data indicates that cumulative net inflows to spot Bitcoin ETFs fell from $57.62 billion on October 29 to $53.51 billion on November 19.

On November 19 alone, these funds recorded $582 million in net outflows, and they took in money on only six trading days between October 23 and November 19. The total net assets of Bitcoin ETFs dropped to $76.55 billion from $104.88 billion on October 28, squeezed by both outflows and declining prices.

Higher interest rates add more pressure. The federal funds rate is the benchmark for overnight loans, and higher rates typically divert investment away from speculative assets like Bitcoin. The Federal Reserve raised its upper limit to 4.00% from 3.75% in September, and markets are bracing for another possible rate hike on December 9. Kendrick has cautioned that if this tightening continues, Bitcoin could drop to about $50,000, 18% below its current price.

Since it closed at $8,118 in November 2017, Bitcoin has grown at an annual compounded rate of about 25%. While this is a strong performance for most assets, it falls short of the 36% annual growth needed to reach the $1 million target.

The last five years have shown even weaker performance. Bitcoin has risen only about 4% since November 2021, despite nearly an 8,000% increase over the past decade. Both our five-year Bitcoin outlook and our look at $1,000 in Bitcoin by 2030 illustrate how much returns have slowed.

Even Bitcoin enthusiasts predict more modest gains going forward. Investor and podcast host Anthony Pompliano remarked on August 19, 2026, “The future return of Bitcoin, I think, is going to be much lower than people have previously experienced. So I don’t think it’s going to compound at 60%, 70% year over year for a decade.”

Bitcoin’s chance of reaching $1 million by 2035 appears low. First, it must recover its all-time high of $126,080, which is 107% above the current price, as our prediction on when Bitcoin gets back there covers. Then spot ETF outflows need to turn into steady inflows, the Fed needs to stop raising rates, and Bitcoin has to compound near 36% a year, faster than it has since 2017.

Bernstein’s $150,000 mid-2027 checkpoint is the first test. If Bitcoin is still below $126,080 by mid-2027 and cumulative ETF inflows keep shrinking from $53.51 billion, the $1 million target could slip well past 2035. But if Bitcoin closes above its old high with weeks of steady ETF inflows, $1 million could return to serious conversation, though the late 2030s still look more likely.

Bitcoin, sometimes called "digital gold," also fell to about $55,100 on Saturday, its lowest level since September 2024, with market commentators like Arthur Hayes predicting a lower low of $5000 .
Goldman Sachs warned that if the market keeps sliding, funds could sell up to $80.6 billion in stocks this week. Even a bounce could trigger $28.6 billion in selling, according to Bloomberg.

Goldman's Panic Index reached 9 out of 10 on Friday. The firm's trading desk expects computer-driven funds to continue selling shares next week, even if the market rallies. Goldman estimates the funds sold $57 billion in equities over the last month and hold a net short position of $19 billion in U.S. stocks.

Analysts at crypto exchange Bitunix said the joint slide is a sign of tight funding and cash requirements, not a weakness in any asset. Sticky U.S. inflation has boosted rate-hike bets, pushing up the dollar and Treasury yields, the analysts added. Selling in AI stocks and the need for cash at year-end have also weighed.

They added that "in the short term, a break below $61,250 could expose BTC to further tests of $60,600 and $60,000. Conversely, a recovery above 62,265-62,720 accompanied by improving CVD would warrant attention to a potential short squeeze."
The CME Group's FedWatch tool showed traders are pricing in an 88.6% chance of a Fed rate hike at its Dec. 8-9 meeting.

Economist Peter Schiff also likened the slide in gold to 2008 when the metal bottomed out months ahead of stocks. If the Fed continues to fight inflation, "stocks, bonds, real estate and crypto will crash much more than gold," he warned on X on Wednesday.

In its note on Friday, Bitunix also highlighted heavy bearish positioning on Hyperliquid (HYPE), a derivatives trading platform. As of Sunday, the biggest pile of leveraged bets for profits was around $55,900, down about 6% on Bitcoin's price at $59,726. Such a drop could flush out those traders and extend the decline.
Smaller pockets of bets against Bitcoin were also found near $61,700 and $62,700.
Bitcoin's price was up over 3% in the past 24 hours. On Stocktwits, it was the top trending ticker among cryptocurrencies at the time of writing.
Retail sentiment around it improved to 'neutral' from the 'bearish' zone, as chatter around it remained at high levels over the past day.

extraction.body: In recent years, people have been increasingly looking for new ways to form platonic connections, as loneliness and social isolation have become more prevalent. In 2023, the U.S. Surgeon General went so far as to label this issue a public health crisis. Remote workers, who miss the everyday interactions found in an office, and younger individuals eager to create their adult social circles based on shared interests and hobbies, are among those seeking meaningful friendships. Thanks to online dating apps, the stigma associated with finding connections online has largely faded away. This has welcomed a new wave of apps focused on fostering friendships and building local communities. According to estimates from Appfigures, over a dozen local-focused friendship apps have collectively generated approximately $16 million in consumer spending in the U.S. so far this year. Some notable examples include Timeleft, Meet5, and Bumble’s BFF. Additionally, these apps have garnered approximately 4.3 million downloads thus far in 2025. The apps aim to provide a less awkward solution than, for instance, approaching a stranger at the gym or local café and trying to strike up a conversation. These platforms clearly indicate that everyone using the app is looking for the same thing — friendship, not romance — making it much less intimidating to initiate conversations. From major players like Meetup to newer ones like 222, there are plenty of apps that cater to the growing demand for meaningful friendships. We’ve compiled a list of them for you to try out. The app 222 is an iOS-only social events platform that facilitates in-person meetups by pairing a group of strangers based on their personality test results. The app sends invitations to nearby public social events, such as wine bars and comedy clubs. There is then a vetting process, and selected participants are notified on the day of the event. A bonus for those who feel socially anxious: You’re allowed to bring a plus-one. BFF is available for free download on iOS and Android devices. Clyx is another emerging app in the group-based social networking landscape, with a strong focus on discovering local events. The social platform helps users find community events by integrating data from platforms like Ticketmaster and TikTok. Additionally, Clyx allows users to upload their contact lists, helping them see which events their friends plan to attend. The app also includes a feature that recommends other users to connect with at these events. As of now, Clyx operates exclusively in two cities: Miami and London. However, it has plans to expand to additional areas in the near future, with New York City and São Paulo at the top of the list. The app is available on the App Store and Google Play Store . Crowdier is a new group social app that lets friend groups connect with others. Users can create a group of 2-5 friends and browse other groups to arrange hangouts in person. To initiate a match, users can “Wave” at groups they like, and if those groups wave back, they can plan in a shared chat. A match requires the majority of both groups to agree. For example, 2 people in a 4-person group needs to say yes. Available on iOS and Android , Les Amís serves cities across Europe, including Amsterdam, Barcelona, Berlin, Madrid, Paris, and Stockholm. In the U.S., the app is available in Austin and New York, with plans to expand to Boston, Miami, and Los Angeles. The app uses a paid membership model that varies by city, with fees of $70 in New York and €55 in Amsterdam. The local event-discovery platform has been around since 2002, helping millions of users connect with others who share similar interests. Users can RSVP to events; join groups that cater to a variety of hobbies, professions, or social causes; and create their own groups and events. They can also chat with group members and post updates and photos from gatherings. This European community-building app recently launched in the U.S., targeting users over 40 who want to meet new people in their area and participate in group activities such as picnics, concerts, and hiking. Notably, in a short time, there have been around 777,000 U.S. downloads so far across the App Store and Google Play Store , according to Appfigures estimates. Pie is another one of the newer social apps on the market. It features an AI-driven quiz designed to predict which users are most likely to be compatible with each other. Each person who RSVPs to a Pie event takes a brief personality assessment, and the algorithm organizes attendees into groups of six, who are then added to a group chat within the Pie app, allowing them to interact with each other before the event. Users can book dinners online or through the app . In terms of pricing, it varies depending on the country and restaurant. Users pay for a ticket up front and are responsible for covering their own dinner and drinks. Washed Up is a social event discovery app that launched in early 2026, designed for people in the Los Angeles area who want an easier way to find things to do and meet new people. The app helps users discover local events, such as concerts, trivia nights, and comedy shows, while also giving them a built-in way to connect with others who plan to attend. Instead of going to events alone, users can create or join “plans,” which are small group meetups tied to specific events. Users can browse these plans and request to join, chat with the group, and add new friends, making it easier to show up to events with people rather than by themselves. It’s available to download on the App Store . Wyzr Friends is an activity-based friendship app designed for adults 40 and older, catering to empty nesters, those who are divorced, and other users seeking to connect with like-minded individuals. Users can thumbs up or down potential friends and arrange in-person activities based on shared interests, such as going to the movies or hiking. It’s available on iOS and Android devices in the U.S., Canada, Australia, Ireland, the Philippines, Singapore, and Mexico. Mmotion is a newly launched friendship app that blends location tracking with social discovery to help users connect with people nearby and explore new bars and restaurants in their area. Upon joining, users can participate in interest-based groups — such as hiking, basketball, or art — view a map of active users, and send messages to those nearby. The app also highlights new places on the map, making it easy to find a restaurant or venue to try. Mmotion is currently only available to users in New York City on iOS and Android devices. Users must first submit an application to be considered. Launched in March 2026, Synchrony is a new social app tailored for neurodivergent adults. Founded by a mother of a son on the autism spectrum, it aims to create a supportive community through features like interest-based matching and two-step identity verification. This ensures that users engage safely, as both a user and a trusted person must verify personal details and a photo ID during registration. A standout feature is Jesse, an optional AI communication tool that assists users in navigating conversations. The AI provides editable prompts to help express thoughts, clarifies conversations, and offers boundary-setting suggestions. While the incorporation of AI may raise concerns, there are guardrails built into Jesse, such as avoiding medical advice. passages: One thing to mention about these apps is that, depending on your employer, restrictions may apply.
Certain companies require corporate apps like Google Meet and Microsoft Teams to run inside an isolated Android Work Profile.
In such situations, Android Auto may block calendar sync or prevent the app from appearing on the screen.
There's a Work Mode in the works on Android Auto , though, so it may soon be easier to reach all those apps that are locked out by your employer.
Because Meet is Google's own app, it fits naturally into the Android Auto experience.
You can see your upcoming meetings on the car display and join a call with a single tap, all in audio-only mode so your eyes stay on the road.
Whether it's a short check-in with your manager or a longer team call, Meet makes it easy to keep up with your schedule even if you have to drive around.
Yes, Android Auto will read out your texts — we all know that.
But it can also handle other apps, reading out your messages if you so desire and then letting you use your voice to reply.
WhatsApp is the clearest example of this working well, as Android Auto can read your messages aloud.
Signal offers similar read-aloud and reply functionality; so do Facebook Messenger, Microsoft Teams and Google Chat, to name a few.
But the platform's compatible app library runs much deeper, well beyond navigation and streaming.
Each one adds layer after layer of functionality that most users never think to explore.
Discovering new apps can genuinely change how you commute while also making it possible to enjoy your drive just a tiny bit more.
Google Maps and other similar tools can surface the nearest gas stations and even tell you the latest prices, but Fuelio gives more in-depth information regarding fuel type, distance and more.
While Fuelio is free to use with Android Auto, there is a premium version available that costs money.
When you're traveling abroad, costs go up by quite a bit, so you should make the most of your home Wi-Fi.
Apps like HERE WeGo through Android Auto offer offline navigation, so your data plan isn't ever a concern.
For some countries, you can download maps for certain areas, such as for Germany where you can grab a map for Berlin and another for Hamburg.
Compatible apps will automatically pop up on your Android Auto launcher.
This free tool (the paid version removes ads) gives you access to a crowd-sourced map that lets you see the nearest charging stations along your route.
Its real strength is the community behind it, because drivers leave real-time feedback, uploading photos of the charger layout, reporting broken plugs and checking in after charging.
That gives you a clear picture of what to expect before you pull in, so a station that looks fine on paper but has been out of service for days won't catch you off guard.

extraction.body: “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes , reached an impressive box office milestone this weekend, becoming one of the few documentaries to make more than $100 million worldwide. Variety reports that almost all of the film’s $102.4 million box office has come from U.S. audiences, from whom it has grossed $93.4 million so far. “You Can See Everything” will be opening in many more countries over the next few months — starting with Mexico, Brazil and Argentina on Nov. 25 and 26 — so its box office total could end up significantly higher. And while the documentary was already an undeniable commercial success for indie studio A24 (especially with a reported budget of $7 million), it could now surpass the records set by the highest grossing documentaries of all time — “March of the Penguins” ($127 million globally) and “Fahrenheit 9/11” ($222 million globally).
